Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?

Qi Wang1    Yun Qu1    Lizhou Cai1    Heming Zou1    Haoang Chi1    Yiqin Lv1    Xiang Li1 Affiliation: Haiyan Feng1, Mengyu Ge2, Yize Geng2, Yuhang Jiang1, Yixiu Mao1, Xiangyang Ji1†
Abstract

Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study conditional interaction, a predict–gate–execute–update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate’s utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching 1/ρu1/\rho_{u}, where ρu\rho_{u} is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: ρu\rho_{u} is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.

1  The Interaction Problem at Scale

Recent advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) (Morris et al., 2024) have largely focused on scaling model capacity, data volume, and computational resources (Sutton, 2019; Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), along with innovations in architectures, pretraining or post-training techniques, retrieval, and inference-time search. A significant portion of this investment has gone to a resource-intensive intelligent system, referred to as System-2, which handles reasoning, planning, decision-making, function calling, or even computer use. As frontier large models (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025), extend compute, and larger collectives of agents emerge, the potential of this executive system grows proportionally with resource availability. However, as systems become more capable, the costs of generating, evaluating, and acting on each additional interaction may become a constraining factor. This presents an alternative scaling challenge: not merely how many interactions a system can manage, but which interactions justify their associated costs.

An interaction encompasses any information exchange between an intelligent system and its data, computations, or environment. It gathers information at a cost: for a large language model (LLM), a generation episode in which a prompt produces tokens, such as a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022); for an embodied or reinforcement-learning agent, a trajectory of states, actions, and rewards; for a tool-using agent, a tool invocation that calls an external resource and integrates its result. Here, we treat interaction as the unit of analysis, recognizing that these operations are not necessarily equivalent in a physical or statistical sense; they share that each incurs resource commitments before observing the outcome and realizes utility only afterward. Even though reasoning models (Guo et al., 2025) and embodied agents (Kim et al., 2024) benefit from increased interactions, the relative returns from each interaction tend to diminish. For instance, tokens that fail to alter the relevant belief state, training rollouts that yield little policy-gradient signal under the selected objective (Yu et al., 2026), and environment steps that reiterate known information all consume valuable resources while providing minimal task-relevant learning signals.

Determining which interactions to execute is a challenge that System-2 cannot resolve autonomously because assessing an interaction’s value must cost considerably less than executing it. This necessitates the co-design of System-1 and System-2, and this work introduces the conditional interaction as a feasible co-design principle: a lightweight System-1 predicts the utility of potential interactions, the resource-intensive System-2 executes only those interactions that exceed a resource-aware threshold, and the resulting outcomes then serve to refine System-1. Because each system shapes the other, the two must be designed together, and this Perspective asks whether such co-design is a promising path toward AGI. Our central hypothesis posits that the density of utility-relevant interactions, denoted as ρu\rho_{u}, rather than the sheer count of interactions alone, serves as a pivotal metric of scaling efficiency. The co-design of System-1 and System-2, as detailed below, indicates a promising approach for scenarios where interactions are costly, exhibit uneven value, and can be anticipated. This framework is based on the premise that low-cost experiments can be conducted and foreseen effectively.

The Closing of the Accumulation Frontier.

The pursuit of accumulating additional data is increasingly difficult. Human-generated data are finite, since pretraining consolidates much of humanity’s recorded text into a single model and the stock of public text may be depleted within this decade (Villalobos et al., 2024), while high-quality data are scarcer still, as the subset that teaches most is only a fraction of that stock. Synthetic data shift the focus from quantity to coverage: they can partially replenish both (Xu et al., 2025), but the space of synthesizable interactions is combinatorially vast, e.g., robotic data alone would require covering scenes, objects, dynamics, lighting, and sensing, so the pertinent question becomes which synthetic interactions are worth their cost. Moreover, some interactions are inherently expensive: in scientific discovery, robotics, and specialized clinical and industrial settings, data are produced one experiment, actuation, or measurement at a time, at the pace of the underlying process, and no amount of computational power can accelerate a chemical reaction. Shifting the focus toward continual, post-deployment adaptation, we can find that self-evolution sharpens rather than alleviates the bottleneck: an agent that interacts indiscriminately exhausts its finite budget on experiences that yield minimal task-relevant learning, so its progress hinges on which interactions it selects, precisely the decision this Perspective examines.

The vanishing marginal return of undirected interactions and complexity of search space.

Neural scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022) illustrate why counting interactions is ineffective. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be cumulative compute, ℒ⁡(𝒞)\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{C}) the loss, and 𝒫=1−ℒ\mathcal{P}=1-\mathcal{L} a performance measure, e.g., any smooth 𝒫=f⁡(ℒ)\mathcal{P}=f(\mathcal{L}) with bounded f′f^{\prime} yields similar conclusions. Under a power law ℒ⁡(𝒞)∝𝒞−α\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{C})\propto\mathcal{C}^{-\alpha}, α>0\alpha>0, the marginal gain from one more unconditional interaction is

ηunc​(t)=d​𝒫d​𝒞|t=−d​ℒd​𝒞|t∝α​𝒞−α−1,\eta_{\text{unc}}(t)\;=\;\frac{d\mathcal{P}}{d\mathcal{C}}\bigg|_{t}\;=\;-\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\mathcal{C}}\bigg|_{t}\;\propto\;\alpha\,\mathcal{C}^{-\alpha-1}, (1)

which vanishes as compute grows. This empirical relation describes diminishing returns on a fixed landscape traversed by undifferentiated interactions; altering which interactions are executed can shift the curve itself, and this Perspective explores that degree of freedom. Information gain is a canonical utility but not a universal one (Definitions 3 and 5). The following two regimes make the gap between interaction count and interaction utility concrete, and show where the waste arises.

The digital regime: intensive computations, wasted rollouts. In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), a reasoning model is post-trained on problems with automatically checkable answers, scoring each sampled thought chain (a rollout) with a low-cost verifier. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025) samples GG responses {og}g=1G\{o_{g}\}_{g=1}^{G} per prompt τ\tau, scores each with reward rgr_{g}, and forms group-relative advantages

AgGRPO​(τ)=rg−μrσr+ϵ,μr=1G​∑g=1Grg,σr2=1G​∑g=1G(rg−μr)2,A_{g}^{\text{GRPO}}(\tau)=\frac{r_{g}-\mu_{r}}{\sigma_{r}+\epsilon},\quad\mu_{r}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}r_{g},\quad\sigma_{r}^{2}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}(r_{g}-\mu_{r})^{2}, (2)

which weight the per-token log-likelihood gradients in a clipped surrogate objective regularized toward a reference policy. When all responses receive the same reward (rg≡μrr_{g}\equiv\mu_{r}), every Ag=0A_{g}=0, rendering the prompt degenerate: it provides no relative policy-gradient signal while consuming GG rollouts. Only prompts of intermediate difficulty yield mixed outcomes, and a substantial fraction of the pool is degenerate (Yu et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026a). Conditional interaction aids in predicting which prompts yield non-zero advantage, thereby optimizing the generation budget.

The physical regime: expensive rollouts in high-dimensional task spaces. In contrast to the digital regime’s cheap interactions, the physical regime is constrained by expensive rollouts: real-world interactions cannot be freely parallelized and consume tangible time tied to physical dynamics. A generalist agent trained by domain randomization performs across a simulation parameter space Ξ⊆ℝd\Xi\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, where the rollouts needed for generalization grow with the effective dimensionality of Ξ\Xi and the complexity of its deployment scenarios. The qualitative insight is that, in high-dimensional spaces, which tasks are evaluated holds equal importance to how many are assessed.

The super parrot hypothesis: AI for AI, and its efficiency issue.

Fig. 2 sketches a trend we call the super parrot hypothesis. The early foundation model first behaves as a “stochastic parrot” (Bender et al., 2021), imitating human text without grounded understanding (Stage 1, roughly 2020–2022); CoT prompting (Wei et al., 2022) and RLVR (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025) then let it develop reasoning that humans can still follow (Stage 2, 2022–2025); and we hypothesize a Stage 3 in which it encodes information in self-coded representations and improves itself through self-evolution, beyond human interpretation. Viewed as a trajectory, this is a trend toward AI for AI: at each stage a larger share of what the system learns from is produced by AI itself, synthetic instructions (Xu et al., 2025), self-generated reasoning traces scored by automatic verifiers, and ultimately self-chosen experiments (Silver and Sutton, 2025). The same trend exhibits the efficiency issue in sharper form. Every self-generated interaction is paid for with the system’s own compute, yet many of them, such as degenerated RLVR prompts, reasoning tokens that leave the answer unchanged, and self-proposed tasks that are already mastered, teach little to the model. Developing a super parrot therefore needs an internal judgment of value before execution, which is precisely the role this Perspective assigns to System-1.

All of the above discussions raise a fundamental Research Question: How can a System-2 be aware of an interaction’s value before execution?

Our position: co-design the two systems, and the conditional interaction decides what the other pays for.

In response, we prioritize architecture over algorithm: give the executive a partner whose job is to judge, and design the two together. This work argues that a major part of the next advance toward AGI and beyond may come from co-designing System-1 and System-2 rather than from scaling System-2 alone: specifying, training, and scaling the two as one system, where System-1 decides what System-2 executes, which executive runs it, how much it may spend, and what it keeps in memory; System-2’s outcomes are System-1’s supervision; and each is sized with the other in view (Section 3). Integrating a cheap predictor with a costly executor introduces three decisions at scale: which prompts, tasks, or requests merit rollouts, trials, or extensive thought chains (compute); which samples, buffers, caches, and context entries should be preserved (storage); and how costly outcomes should adjust the inexpensive judgment that allocated them (feedback).

This work proposes conditional interaction as a coupling mechanism that allocates interactions based on predicted utility, explicitly optimizing to avoid those predicted to fall below a certain threshold. This perspective applies to diverse applications, including online prompt selection in reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Qu et al., 2026a), task selection in embodied agents (Qu et al., 2025), model routing, and adaptive inference (Li et al., 2026) (Section 2.3). The same pattern applies in a deployed system, where the ledger records inference compute and real-world actions rather than gradient updates (Snell et al., 2024). The transfer focuses on the decision pattern and the scope is intentionally confined to situations with a reliable utility predictor, as this principle does not substitute exploration when the predictor is uncertain (Section 2.4).

ρu\rho_{u}: an efficiency coordinate to scale limited resource.

Classical scaling laws express performance 𝒫\mathcal{P} through parameters NN, data DD, and compute 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The density of utility-relevant interactions ρu\rho_{u}, the fraction of candidate interactions whose utility uu clears a declared floor uminu_{\min} in Eq. (14), is not an additional resource but an efficiency coordinate 𝒫=f⁡(N,D,𝒞,ρu)\mathcal{P}=f(N,D,\mathcal{C};\rho_{u}) describing how well the three convert into capability, generated by the learning dynamics rather than supplied externally. For the canonical utility, Bayesian information gain, ρu\rho_{u} is the informative interaction density ρinfo\rho_{\mathrm{info}}, a special case of the general ρu\rho_{u} in which every formal result is stated; every statement is nonetheless relative to a declared utility, since the densities of prompts with non-zero GRPO advantage, of tasks above an adaptation-risk threshold, and of queries whose answer improves with more compute are different quantities and are not interchangeable.

Uninformative interactions waste both computation and the data slots they occupy, so the effective resources under unconditional training are discounted as ρu​D\rho_{u}D and ρu​𝒞\rho_{u}\mathcal{C}. The compute discount is a direct accounting identity; ρu​D\rho_{u}D is a proposed measure of utility-relevant data consumed, not a smaller available corpus, which a gate leaves unchanged. Two interpretations of this fraction must be kept apart. The pool fraction ρu​(θt)\rho_{u}(\theta_{t}) is a property of the candidate distribution at the current state, produced by the learning dynamics, and no gate can change it; the executed fraction is the share of interactions actually paid for that are informative. Unconditional training executes the pool, so the two coincide, while a perfect gate drives the executed fraction to one. Conditional interaction raises the executed fraction, so that at fixed NN, DD and 𝒞\mathcal{C} more of the budget tends to buy utility-relevant interactions and, hypothetically, as a dynamic account of the exponent. Note that ρu\rho_{u} depends on the policy state, it is not a free axis.

A potentially tighter Cost–QoS–Intelligence frontier.

Directing interactions by predicted utility can tighten the Pareto frontier over compute, data, and model complexity: For example, under the assumptions of Proposition 24, a target is probably reached with less compute, or a fixed budget yields more performance. Suppressing the uninformative fraction 1−ρu1-\rho_{u} acts on every axis at once, since fewer rollouts and gradient reduce compute and data, and routing each task only to the System-2 models it needs cuts the capacity activated per task. The same holds at deployment: training-time gating lowers cost, test-time gating improves quality of service with lowers latency, and concentrating both on informative interactions raises task success per unit of either, so the co-designed pair aims at a frontier that improves on scaling System-2 alone on all three (See Fig. 3), the comprehensive co-design objective.

What we claim, and with what confidence.

Throughout this work, the claim hierarchy is as follows. (i) Premise: future digital and robotic systems may be limited by interaction efficiency more than by parameters or data. (ii) Position: progress toward general intelligence should co-design a cheap System-1 with a costly System-2, coupled by a strategy that values interactions before execution and suppresses those predicted to be uninformative. (iii) Hypothesis: the density of utility-relevant interactions ρu\rho_{u} (ρinfo\rho_{\mathrm{info}} for information gain) is an important determinant of how efficiently resources become capability. (iv) Prediction: ρu\rho_{u} decays as the system improves, and this decay may account for part of the diminishing returns and of the scaling exponent, so that scaling laws are better described in informative compute than in compute alone.

The rest of this Perspective proceeds as follows: formalizing the predict–gate–execute–update loop to implement the conditional interaction (Section 2); building and co-scaling the two subsystems (Section 3); deriving the loop’s screening and regret properties, and why a lightweight System-1 can provide them (Section 4); instantiating the framework across digital training, physical adaptation, test-time computation and agentic use (Sections 5 and 6); and formulating informative compute as a scaling hypothesis (Section 7).

2  Conditional Interaction as A Co-Design Strategy: Predict Before You Pay

Co-design requires an interface: a precise statement of what System-1 judges, what System-2 executes as a resource-intensive operation, and what flows back. Conditional interaction is that interface. Both systems are defined by execution role rather than model family: System-1 is a lightweight, semantic-aware module that takes a candidate interaction as input, e.g., a prompt, task configuration, query, or tool call, with its context and returns a score rather than a solution, and it is consulted on every candidate at a cost cpred≪cexecc_{\text{pred}}\ll c_{\text{exec}}. System-2 is the resource-demanding model or agent that performs the interaction, and is invoked only on the candidates System-1 certifies. The loop runs in both directions, making it co-design rather than a filter bolted onto a finished executive: System-1 shapes the data and effort System-2 receives, and System-2’s outcomes become System-1’s supervision. AlphaZero illustrates this, since its play comes not from deeper search alone but from a policy-value network and a tree search that trained each other (Silver et al., 2018): a more capable System-2 raises the intelligence of accomplishing tasks, while a well-calibrated System-1 determines how much of it is reached per unit of cost and latency (See Fig. 3).

Static cascades versus adaptive co-design.

The pairing can be built in two ways (See Fig. 4). In a static cascade, a standalone fast model classifies each request and hands the hard minority to a large model; Jev, a commercial model described by its developers as a “System One” (TypeSafe AI, 2026), is a clear instance, returning calibrated probabilities over answers defined in advance (Osman, 2026). Such products illustrate commercial interest in fast, structured judgment models compatible with the System-1 role, although a single product does not establish an industry-wide convergence. A static cascade is, by construction, trained once, routes only at the inference layer, and does not receive System-2’s outcomes, which suffices when its predictions are stationary but fails here, because how informative an interaction is for the current System-2 changes with every update. In co-design, System-1 instead predicts utility such as difficulty or learning value relative to the current System-2; it acts in training as well as at inference, scheduling compute and storage such as rollout budgets, replay buffers, batches, key–value (KV) caches, context windows, rather than a single call path. System-2’s realized rewards, gradients, and outcomes recalibrate System-1 online (See Fig. 5). A cascade retrained online on its outcomes moves toward co-design, so the distinction is not the presence of two models but feedback and joint optimization.

2.1  Core Definition

Definition 1 (Conditional Interaction Policy).

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the space of feasible interactions, ℋt={(is,os)}s=0t−1\mathcal{H}_{t}=\{(i_{s},o_{s})\}_{s=0}^{t-1} the history of interaction–outcome pairs, and u^:ℐ×ℋ∗→ℝ\hat{u}:\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{H}^{*}\to\mathbb{R} a predicted utility. A conditional interaction policy is the selection rule

πCI(it∣ℋ0:t)\displaystyle\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}(i_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}) =1Ztexp(βu^(it∣ℋ0:t))⋅[u^(it∣ℋ0:t)≥κt],\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{1}{Z_{t}}\,\exp\!\bigl(\beta\,\hat{u}(i_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\bigr)\,\cdot\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{u}(i_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\geq\kappa_{t}\right], (3a)
Zt\displaystyle Z_{t} =∑i∈ℐexp(βu^(i∣ℋ0:t))[u^(i∣ℋ0:t)≥κt],\displaystyle\;=\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\exp\!\bigl(\beta\,\hat{u}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\bigr)\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{u}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\geq\kappa_{t}\right], (3b)

where β>0\beta>0 controls selection sharpness, κt\kappa_{t} is a utility threshold enforcing a minimum predicted utility, and ZtZ_{t} is a sum for finite ℐ\mathcal{I}, or an integral against a base measure on a continuous ℐ\mathcal{I} to normalize πCI\pi_{\mathrm{CI}} over the admissible set {i:u^≥κt}\{i:\hat{u}\geq\kappa_{t}\}. When the admissible set is empty (Zt=0Z_{t}=0), the policy selects an explicit abstention action ∅\varnothing with probability one and executes nothing at step tt; πCI\pi_{\mathrm{CI}} is thus a distribution on ℐ∪{∅}\mathcal{I}\cup\{\varnothing\}. The score u^\hat{u} is a predicted gross utility, which is the right ranking signal when execution costs are equal; when they differ, the policy is applied to the cost-adjusted score u~\tilde{u} of Eq. (16). Score-based results (the greedy limit, the threshold rule, the regret bounds and Lemma 21) then apply to u~\tilde{u} provided the true score is redefined consistently as u−λ​𝒞u-\lambda\mathcal{C}, with relevance, error rates and regret all measured on that net score. Results on the IIE and on ρu\rho_{u} keep their gross-utility definitions unless explicitly redefined; a gate that is accurate for the net score need not have the same error rates with respect to uu.

Interpretation. The indicator in Eq. (3a) restricts the search space by suppressing candidates whose predicted utility falls too far below the current budget. At the same time, the exponential factor sets how sharply the policy concentrates on the best feasible candidates, and hence how much it explores among them. This work reserves gate for this mechanism in prose and uses selection policy to denote πCI\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}. We call the resulting closed loop — predict, gate, execute, and fold the outcome back into the predictor — the predict-then-gate architecture (See Fig. 5); every instance shares it in this Perspective, whatever utility fills and whatever ledger it is scored against.

From soft gating to greedy selection: limiting regimes of the policy.

The two parameters of Eq. (3) play distinct roles: the threshold κt\kappa_{t} decides which interactions are admissible, and the inverse temperature β\beta decides how sharply the policy prefers the best admissible one. The threshold is a statement about utility, not about budget; a budget enters through a price, since in the master objective, i.e., Eq. (15), a multiplier λ\lambda on cost turns the threshold into the cost-dependent rule u^​(i)≥λ​𝒞​(i)\hat{u}(i)\geq\lambda\mathcal{C}(i), and the adaptive update Eq. (22) is one way of setting κt\kappa_{t} so that a target admission rate is met. Write u^t(i)=u^(i∣ℋ0:t)\hat{u}_{t}(i)=\hat{u}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}), and let

denote the admissible set, the largest predicted utility, and the set of maximizers (assumed finite and attained).

Definition 3 (Interaction Utility).

As a running example we take the expected Bayesian surprise (Itti and Baldi, 2005): the utility of interaction ii at executive state θt\theta_{t} is the expected posterior-to-prior divergence it induces,

u(i;θt)≜𝔼[DKL[p(θ∣ℋ0:t,i,o)∥p(θ∣ℋ0:t)]|ℋ0:t,i],u(i;\theta_{t})\;\triangleq\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[p(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t},i,o)\,\Big\|\,p(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\right]\;\big|\;\mathcal{H}_{0:t},i\,\right], (7)

with the expectation over the predictive distribution of the outcome oo. It answers: if I execute this interaction and observe its outcome, how much will my belief change? Interactions with predictable outcomes score near zero; utility measures the magnitude of the belief update, not difficulty or novelty. It is the conditional mutual information I(θ;o∣i,ℋ0:t)I(\theta;o\mid i,\mathcal{H}_{0:t}), which, when the relevant entropies are finite, equals the expected reduction in the entropy of θ\theta. The predictor u^\hat{u} in Eq. (3) estimates whatever utility fills this slot; information gain is one possible choice of uu, not the universal definition of usefulness. Different contexts require different utilities:

u(i)={I⁡(θ;o∣i)(exploration / experiment design),𝔼⁡[Δ​J∣i](expected improvement in curriculum learning),VoI⁡(i)=𝔼⁡[Δ​V∣i](decision making: value of information),ℛadapt​(i,θt)(robust domain randomization / meta learning risk)u(i)=\begin{cases}I(\theta;o\mid i)&\text{(exploration / experiment design),}\\[2.0pt] \mathbb{E}[\Delta J\mid i]&\text{(expected improvement in curriculum learning),}\\[2.0pt] \mathrm{VoI}(i)=\mathbb{E}[\Delta V\mid i]&\text{(decision making: value of information),}\\[2.0pt] \mathcal{R}_{\text{adapt}}(i;\theta_{t})&\text{(robust domain randomization / meta learning risk)}\end{cases} (8)

Their maximizers generally vary case by case. Eq. (7) coincides with the first line (Remark 4) and, combined with a cost, underlies the third; the fourth encodes adaptation risk, and the second is the objective that predictive task samplers estimate directly. Two conventions keep these lines consistent with the master objective of Section 2.3. First, every uu is a gross utility: cost never enters uu and is charged once, through the ledger 𝒞⁡(i)\mathcal{C}(i) and its price λ\lambda, so the value of information becomes net of cost only through that charge. Second, the fourth line is an acquisition score, not the training objective: a robust learner minimizes the tail risk CVaRν\CVaR_{\nu} of Eq. (64), and to do so it prioritizes the tasks with the largest predicted adaptation risk ℛadapt\mathcal{R}_{\text{adapt}} of Eq. (63), the score maximized in Eq. (65). We do not merge these utilities. What they share is the predict-then-gate architecture, and the efficiency results below (screening gain, regret bounds, rescaling) hold for any of them, given the predictor’s ranking quality and the cost asymmetry.

Remark 4 (Representation invariance).

The KL divergence is invariant under invertible reparameterizations of θ\theta, and u(i;θt)=I(θ;o∣i,ℋ0:t)u(i;\theta_{t})=I(\theta;o\mid i,\mathcal{H}_{0:t}) is also invariant under invertible transformations of oo. Hence the utility, and the IIE of Eq. (9), do not depend on the chosen coordinates.

Remark 5 (Scope of the utility).

Eq. (7) measures belief change, not task success, descent direction, or robustness, and coincides with each only under conditions: (a) inference success, only under uniform outcome preferences (Proposition 20); (b) the post-training update direction, only through Fisher (natural-gradient) preconditioning, so an uncertain but noisy interaction need not help (Qu et al., 2026a; Zou et al., 2025); (c) robust adaptation, only when evaluated on the tail, as in the CVaR adaptation risk of Eqs. (63) and (64) in Appendix B (Qu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). Conversely, an interaction that barely moves the posterior can still be valuable: it may confirm a belief, test robustness, improve calibration, avert a rare failure, or inform another agent. Information gain, learning progress, decision value and task improvement are therefore distinct quantities, and conditional interaction is always relative to whichever one is declared.

2.2  The Interaction Information Efficiency Metric

Definition 6 (Interaction Information Efficiency).

For a stream of TT screened candidates i0,…,iT−1i_{0},\dots,i_{T-1}, the Interaction Information Efficiency (IIE) is the utility obtained per unit of system-level cost,

IIET=∑t=0T−1𝕀⁡(it)​[it​ executed]∑t=0T−1(cpred​(it)+𝒞⁡(it)​[it​ executed]),\mathrm{IIE}_{T}\;=\;\frac{\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\,\mathbb{I}(i_{t})\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[i_{t}\text{ executed}\right]}{\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\,\bigl(c_{\text{pred}}(i_{t})+\mathcal{C}(i_{t})\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[i_{t}\text{ executed}\right]\bigr)}, (9)

where 𝕀⁡(it)=u⁡(it,θt)\mathbb{I}(i_{t})=u(i_{t};\theta_{t}) is the declared utility (the expected Bayesian surprise of Eq. (7) in the canonical case), 𝒞⁡(it)\mathcal{C}(i_{t}) the execution cost, and cpred​(it)c_{\text{pred}}(i_{t}) the cost of screening the candidate, paid whether or not it is executed (zero for unconditional interaction); it is the full per-candidate screening cost, encoding plus scoring, which Proposition 14 splits as cscreen=cembed+cscorec_{\text{screen}}=c_{\text{embed}}+c_{\text{score}}. Predictor refitting and audit executions are amortized system costs, reported separately (Section 4.1). Because a ratio can be raised by obtaining very little at very low cost, IIE is always reported together with the yield, the utility obtained per screened candidate,

YT=1T​∑t=0T−1𝕀⁡(it)​[it​ executed].Y_{T}\;=\;\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{I}(i_{t})\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[i_{t}\text{ executed}\right]. (10)

Both are empirical estimates, over a finite stream, of population quantities for candidates i∼𝒟i\sim\mathcal{D}; for the IIE,

IIEpop=𝔼​[𝕀​(i)​[i​ executed]]𝔼⁡[cpred​(i)+𝒞⁡(i)​[i​ executed]],\mathrm{IIE}_{\mathrm{pop}}\;=\;\frac{\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbb{I}(i)\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[i\text{ executed}\right]\bigr]}{\mathbb{E}\bigl[c_{\text{pred}}(i)+\mathcal{C}(i)\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[i\text{ executed}\right]\bigr]}, (11)

and IIET→IIEpop\mathrm{IIE}_{T}\to\mathrm{IIE}_{\mathrm{pop}} almost surely for an i.i.d. stream, by the strong law of large numbers applied to numerator and denominator. A ratio of random sums is not the ratio of their expectations at finite TT, so the results below are stated for IIEpop\mathrm{IIE}_{\mathrm{pop}}; they hold exactly for a fixed pool when fractions and class means are taken over that pool.

Notation: ρu\rho_{u} in general, ρinfo\rho_{\mathrm{info}} as a special case.

Every proposition, theorem and corollary below is stated for a general declared utility uu and its density of utility-relevant interactions ρu\rho_{u}, the fraction of candidates whose true utility clears a floor uminu_{\min} fixed in advance (Eq. (14)); candidates below the floor are called dead. The informative interaction density ρinfo\rho_{\mathrm{info}} is the special case in which uu is the expected information gain of Eq. (7): there “utility-relevant” reads “informative”, 𝕀\mathbb{I} is the expected Bayesian surprise, and utilities are measured in nats. No result below relies on that choice unless it says so.

Partition the candidate pool into the utility-relevant fraction ρu\rho_{u}, with mean utility 𝕀¯rel\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}} and mean cost 𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}, and the dead fraction 1−ρu1-\rho_{u}, with mean utility 𝕀¯dead\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}} and mean cost 𝒞¯dead\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}. Pool averages are 𝕀¯=ρu​𝕀¯rel+(1−ρu)​𝕀¯dead\bar{\mathbb{I}}=\rho_{u}\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}+(1-\rho_{u})\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}} and 𝒞¯=ρu​𝒞¯rel+(1−ρu)​𝒞¯dead\bar{\mathcal{C}}=\rho_{u}\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}+(1-\rho_{u})\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}, and unconditional interaction attains IIEunc=𝕀¯/𝒞¯\mathrm{IIE}^{\text{unc}}=\bar{\mathbb{I}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}.

Proposition 7 (IIE Gain).

Assume dead candidates carry no utility (𝕀¯dead=0\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}}=0, as when umin→0+u_{\min}\to 0^{+} for a non-negative utility), and use the system-level ledger of Eq. (9), in its population form Eq. (11), which charges a predictor cost cpredc_{\text{pred}} to every screened candidate.

  1. 1.

    (Perfect, free predictor.) If exactly the utility-relevant candidates are executed and cpred=0c_{\text{pred}}=0,

    IIECIIIEunc=𝕀¯rel/𝒞¯rel𝕀¯/𝒞¯=1ρu⋅𝒞¯𝒞¯rel= 1+1−ρuρu⋅𝒞¯dead𝒞¯rel,\frac{\mathrm{IIE}^{\mathrm{CI}}}{\mathrm{IIE}^{\text{unc}}}\;=\;\frac{\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}{\bar{\mathbb{I}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}}\;=\;\frac{1}{\rho_{u}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}\;=\;1+\frac{1-\rho_{u}}{\rho_{u}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}, (12)

    which equals 1/ρu1/\rho_{u} when 𝒞¯dead=𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}=\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}} and exceeds it if and only if 𝒞¯dead>𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}>\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}.

  2. 2.

    (Imperfect, costly predictor.) With class-conditional false-positive rate fp\mathrm{fp} (the fraction of dead candidates admitted) and false-negative rate fn\mathrm{fn} (the fraction of utility-relevant candidates suppressed),

    IIECIIIEunc=𝕀¯rel/𝒞¯rel𝕀¯/𝒞¯⋅(1+fp⁡(1−ρu)​𝒞¯dead+cpred(1−fn)​ρu​𝒞¯rel)−1,\frac{\mathrm{IIE}^{\mathrm{CI}}}{\mathrm{IIE}^{\text{unc}}}\;=\;\frac{\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}{\bar{\mathbb{I}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}}\cdot\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{fp}\,(1-\rho_{u})\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}+c_{\text{pred}}}{(1-\mathrm{fn})\,\rho_{u}\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}\right)^{-1}, (13)

    which is non-increasing in each of fp\mathrm{fp}, fn\mathrm{fn} and cpredc_{\text{pred}}, strictly decreasing in any of them whose coefficient is positive, and recovers Eq. (12) as fp,cpred→0\mathrm{fp},c_{\text{pred}}\to 0.

False negatives do not dilute the IIE ratio directly, since suppressed interactions are simply not paid for; they enter by spreading screening and false-positive costs over fewer utility-relevant executions and, more importantly, by reducing the yield Eq. (10) by the factor 1−fn1-\mathrm{fn}. Efficiency and yield must therefore be reported together: an aggressive gate can raise IIE while starving the learner of signal. With ρu≪1\rho_{u}\ll 1, small error rates, and cpred≪𝒞¯relc_{\text{pred}}\ll\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}, the realized multiplier remains substantial, consistent with the several-fold rollout savings reported for predictive prompt sampling (Qu et al., 2026a), but these are ideal values, not guarantees. Under equal execution costs and perfect screening, 1/ρu1/\rho_{u} is the benchmark for the IIE gain; with heterogeneous costs the ideal gain is Eq. (12) itself, which exceeds 1/ρu1/\rho_{u} when dead interactions cost more than relevant ones. The zero-utility assumption on dead candidates matters once umin>0u_{\min}>0: if they retain a mean utility 𝕀¯dead>0\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}}>0, the first equality of Eq. (12) still holds, but the ideal ratio becomes 1ρu​𝒞¯𝒞¯rel​(1−(1−ρu)​𝕀¯dead/𝕀¯)\frac{1}{\rho_{u}}\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}\bigl(1-(1-\rho_{u})\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}}/\bar{\mathbb{I}}\bigr), so the closed forms of Eq. (12) become upper bounds (Section A.2), and 1/ρu1/\rho_{u} bounds the gain only when, in addition, 𝒞¯dead≤𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}\leq\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}.

Remark 8 (Cost-correlated errors).

Eq. (13) assumes error rates independent of cost. If errors concentrate on expensive interactions, the false-positive cost becomes ∫fp⁡(𝒞)​𝒞​d​Fdead​(𝒞)>fp​𝒞¯dead\int\mathrm{fp}(\mathcal{C})\,\mathcal{C}\,dF_{\text{dead}}(\mathcal{C})>\mathrm{fp}\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}, so validation should report cost-conditioned rates.

Remark 9 (Identifiability of ρu\rho_{u}).

Fitting ρu\rho_{u} to a loss curve is circular, since ℒ=a​(ρ⁡(𝒞)​𝒞)−α′\mathcal{L}=a(\rho(\mathcal{C})\mathcal{C})^{-\alpha^{\prime}} with ρ⁡(𝒞)=𝒞s\rho(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C}^{s} fits any exponent. We therefore measure it independently: for a declared utility uu and a threshold umin>0u_{\min}>0 fixed a priori,

ρu(θt)=Pri∼𝒟[u(i;θt)≥umin],\rho_{u}(\theta_{t})\;=\;\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\bigl[\,u(i;\theta_{t})\geq u_{\min}\,\bigr], (14)

with uu the true utility estimated from executed interactions, not the predictor’s u^ϕ\hat{u}_{\phi}; ρinfo\rho_{\mathrm{info}} denotes ρu\rho_{u} for the information-gain utility, and densities under different utilities are not comparable. In RLVR the natural declared utility is the probability that a group of GG rollouts has mixed rewards, uadv​(τ,θt)=1−pτG−(1−pτ)Gu_{\mathrm{adv}}(\tau;\theta_{t})=1-p_{\tau}^{G}-(1-p_{\tau})^{G} with pτp_{\tau} the current pass rate; with umin→0+u_{\min}\to 0^{+}, ρu\rho_{u} becomes ρadv\rho_{\mathrm{adv}}, the fraction of prompts that can yield a non-zero GRPO advantage. This is a proxy for useful policy-gradient signal, not for information gain: an all-fail group still informs a posterior over the prompt’s difficulty, and a mixed group can give a noisy update, so ρadv\rho_{\mathrm{adv}} and ρinfo\rho_{\mathrm{info}} are distinct densities. In the physical regime ρu\rho_{u} is the fraction of tasks whose adaptation risk exceeds uminu_{\min}. Because ρu\rho_{u} depends on (u,umin)(u,u_{\min}), the meaningful object is its relative decay ρu​(θt)/ρu​(θ0)\rho_{u}(\theta_{t})/\rho_{u}(\theta_{0}). We propose its agreement across thresholds and across proxies such as the expected gradient norm or the learnability score ∂t𝔼[r∣τ,θt]\partial_{t}\mathbb{E}[r\mid\tau,\theta_{t}] as a robustness diagnostic, not a theoretical invariance: tail probabilities at different thresholds need not decay proportionally, and gradient norm and learning progress are not equivalent. Measurement also needs a protocol. Because the gate censors what is observed (Section 7.2), ρu\rho_{u} is estimated on an audit pool drawn from 𝒟\mathcal{D} independently of the gate, with repeated rollouts per candidate, confidence intervals, and re-estimation as θt\theta_{t} changes.

2.3  A Master Objective and Its Special Cases

Conditional interaction provides a common predict-then-gate architecture for online prompt selection in LLM post-training, active domain randomization for Sim2Real transfer, and adaptive experimental design in AI for science. The unification is one of architecture, not of objective. What elevates the family from heuristics to a scaling lens is (i) suppression as a first-class objective, (ii) predictive amortization, i.e., estimating utility before execution, and (iii) generality across interaction types, cost structures, policy representations, and reward topologies. On its own, this is a family resemblance; to formalize the claim, we state one optimization problem and obtain each technique by instantiating its variables, including the utility that fills the gating slot.

Definition 10 (Master Conditional-Interaction Objective).

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be a finite menu of candidates with predicted utility u^​(i)\hat{u}(i) and cost 𝒞⁡(i)>0\mathcal{C}(i)>0, and let x⁡(i)∈[0,1]x(i)\in[0,1] be the probability of executing candidate ii. The master objective maximizes expected executed utility under a cost budget Γ\Gamma:

x⋆=arg​maxx∈[0,1]ℐ∑i∈ℐx(i)u^(i)s.t.∑i∈ℐx(i)𝒞(i)≤Γ.x^{\star}\;=\;\argmax_{x\in[0,1]^{\mathcal{I}}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}x(i)\,\hat{u}(i)\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}x(i)\,\mathcal{C}(i)\leq\Gamma. (15)

This is a fractional knapsack. For a multiplier λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 its Lagrangian ∑ix⁡(i)​(u^​(i)−λ​𝒞​(i))\sum_{i}x(i)\bigl(\hat{u}(i)-\lambda\mathcal{C}(i)\bigr) is maximized by the threshold rule x⋆(i)=[u^(i)≥λ𝒞(i)]x^{\star}(i)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{u}(i)\geq\lambda\mathcal{C}(i)\right], i.e. by admitting candidates in order of value per unit cost u^​(i)/𝒞​(i)\hat{u}(i)/\mathcal{C}(i), with λ\lambda fixed by the budget (at most one candidate is fractional at the optimum). The threshold rule is the gate of Eq. (3) with the cost-dependent threshold λ​𝒞​(i)\lambda\mathcal{C}(i), which reduces to a common κt=λ​𝒞¯\kappa_{t}=\lambda\bar{\mathcal{C}} when costs are equal. Adding an entropy regularizer β−1​∑iHb​(x⁡(i))\beta^{-1}\sum_{i}H_{b}(x(i)) softens the gate into x⋆​(i)=σ⁡(β⁡(u^​(i)−λ​𝒞​(i)))x^{\star}(i)=\sigma\bigl(\beta(\hat{u}(i)-\lambda\mathcal{C}(i))\bigr), with σ\sigma the logistic function, of which Eq. (3) applied to the cost-adjusted score is the normalized sampling analogue. A cardinality constraint ∑ix⁡(i)=B\sum_{i}x(i)=B with integral xx gives the top-BB batch problem, which differs from independent thresholding only when utilities interact (redundancy among co-selected candidates), captured by the diversity term of Eq. (47).

Gross utility, net value, and three selection rules.

With the cost-adjusted (net) score

u~​(i)=u^​(i)−λ​𝒞​(i),\tilde{u}(i)\;=\;\hat{u}(i)-\lambda\,\mathcal{C}(i), (16)

three rules must be kept apart when costs differ. (a) The budgeted batch rule of Eq. (15) admits every candidate with u~​(i)≥0\tilde{u}(i)\geq 0, i.e. with value per unit cost u^​(i)/𝒞​(i)≥λ\hat{u}(i)/\mathcal{C}(i)\geq\lambda. (b) The single-draw net-value rule selects arg​maxi⁡u~​(i)\argmax_{i}\tilde{u}(i), as in Eq. (33). (c) The policy of Eq. (3) applied to the raw score u^\hat{u} selects arg​maxi⁡u^​(i)\argmax_{i}\hat{u}(i) in its greedy limit (Proposition 2). When costs are equal the three rank candidates identically, by u^\hat{u}, although (a) selects a set and (b) and (c) a single candidate. When they differ, (c) can contradict (a) and (b): the candidate with the largest raw utility need not have the largest net value or value per unit cost. Applying Eq. (3) to u~\tilde{u} with κt=0\kappa_{t}=0 removes the conflict: its admissible set is exactly the solution of (a), up to the one fractional item, and its greedy limit is (b). We therefore use the raw score only when costs are equal, and u~\tilde{u} otherwise.

The techniques discussed here arise by choosing ℐ\mathcal{I}, u^\hat{u}, and 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In agentic interaction selection (Sections 5, 6.1 and 6.3), ℐ\mathcal{I} is the task or prompt pool, the reasoning increments available for a query, or the tool/think/ask menu; u^\hat{u} is adaptation risk, prompt informativeness, or expected reduction in answer uncertainty; and 𝒞\mathcal{C} is rollout cost, inference compute, or a composite of latency, money, tokens, and risk, so that Eq. (15) becomes risk-prioritized sampling, adaptive halting, or the agentic gate. In the orchestration of System-2 executives (Section 3), System-1 interprets a task semantically before any of it is executed and can therefore also decide who should execute it and how much they may spend: ℐ\mathcal{I} is the pool of available System-2 models or agents together with their compute budgets, u^\hat{u} their predicted contribution, and 𝒞\mathcal{C} their inference cost, so Eq. (15) is a joint routing and budget-allocation rule; token-level mixture-of-experts layers and dynamic depth are the same decision at finer granularity. Eq. (15) captures the selection structure these methods share, not the interchangeability of their learning dynamics or guarantees.

2.4  Scope: When Gating Is and Is Not Justified

The principle applies only where interactions are individually costly, heterogeneous in informativeness, and predictable before execution by a model cheaper than execution itself. Gating has no guaranteed advantage when candidates are homogeneous in utility, when predicting their utility costs about as much as executing them, or when execution is cheap. Dense pretraining, minibatch stochastic gradient descent over independent, identically distributed data, and static supervised learning often come close to these conditions, but need not: a fixed corpus can hold examples whose value differs and is predictable from cheap features, which data-selection methods exploit. A gain observed there calls for an accounting of where it comes from, not a refutation of the principle. Within that regime, gating is justified when a predictor exists whose cost is well below execution cost and whose error εϕ\varepsilon_{\phi} is small relative to the utility gaps it must resolve (Theorem 18).

It should be relaxed, executing uncertain or even predicted-uninformative interactions, when: (1) the predictor is poorly calibrated or off-distribution, since its blind spots are where it wrongly suppresses; (2) interactions carry option or exploratory value not captured by one-step utility; (3) prediction costs about as much as execution, voiding Proposition 14; (4) false negatives are catastrophic (safety-critical control, irreversible actions); or (5) the utility is misspecified, so that the predictor systematically suppresses the very interactions that would reveal the misspecification.

In such regimes the right object is an exploratory value of information, e.g. an upper-confidence or Thompson criterion, replacing u^\hat{u} in Eq. (15) with u^+c​σϕ\hat{u}+c\,\sigma_{\phi}, which recovers pure exploitation as c→0c\to 0 and uncertainty-seeking exploration, dominated by σϕ\sigma_{\phi}, as c→∞c\to\infty. That limit favours the most uncertain candidates rather than sampling the pool uniformly; undirected exploration needs a separate mixture with a uniform policy, as in Section 7.2; the uncertainty-aware acquisition functionals of Eqs. (65) and (62) (Appendix B) are the mechanism by which the principle avoids over-pruning. Conditional interaction is a statement about how to spend a trustworthy informativeness signal, not a claim that one always exists. Regimes (1) and (5) are the most insidious, since the predictor’s errors concentrate precisely where it has no data and the interactions that would reveal them are never executed; the audit sampling described after Proposition 14 is the minimal safeguard, and Section 7.2 treats this censoring formally.

3  Co-Designing the Two Systems: Architecture and Co-Scaling

Section 2 specified what System-1 decides and how its decisions are scored. Once the predictor exists, three questions follow: how should it be trained, how accurate must it be, and how should its capacity scale with the executor? We address them in turn.

3.1  The Two Systems as an Operator Decomposition

Let θ\theta and ϕ\phi be the executive and predictive parameters. Define

𝒯exec​(θ,ϕ,ℋ)\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\text{exec}}(\theta,\phi;\,\mathcal{H}) =(θ−ηθ𝔼i∼πCI(⋅∣ℋ;ϕ)[∇θℒ(θ,i)]+ξθ,ϕ),\displaystyle=\Bigl(\theta-\eta_{\theta}\,\mathbb{E}_{i\sim\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H};\phi)}\!\left[\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta,i)\right]+\xi_{\theta},\;\;\phi\Bigr), (17)
𝒯pred​(θ,ϕ,ℋ)\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\text{pred}}(\theta,\phi;\,\mathcal{H}) =(θ,ϕ−ηϕ​∇ϕ𝔼i∈ℋ​[d⁡(u^ϕ​(i,ℋ),u⁡(i,θ))]+ξϕ),\displaystyle=\Bigl(\theta,\;\;\phi-\eta_{\phi}\,\nabla_{\phi}\,\mathbb{E}_{i\in\mathcal{H}}\!\bigl[d(\hat{u}_{\phi}(i;\mathcal{H}),\,u(i;\theta))\bigr]+\xi_{\phi}\Bigr), (18)

where dd is a strictly proper scoring rule (e.g. squared error or log loss) and ξθ,ξϕ\xi_{\theta},\xi_{\phi} are stochastic-gradient noise. 𝒯exec\mathcal{T}_{\text{exec}} improves the policy along gradients sampled through the gate; 𝒯pred\mathcal{T}_{\text{pred}} fits the predictor to realized utilities. Each operator maps the pair (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) to a pair and updates one component, so their composition is well defined: System-1 is refitted first, and System-2 then steps along gradients sampled through the refitted gate.

Definition 11 (Conditional-Interaction Operator Decomposition).

A conditional-interaction architecture is any learning system whose update can be written as

(θt+1,ϕt+1)=(𝒯exec∘𝒯pred)(θt,ϕt;ℋ0:t),(\theta_{t+1},\phi_{t+1})\;=\;\bigl(\mathcal{T}_{\text{exec}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\text{pred}}\bigr)(\theta_{t},\phi_{t};\mathcal{H}_{0:t}), (19)

with πCI\pi_{\mathrm{CI}} satisfying Definition 1 for u^=u^ϕ\hat{u}=\hat{u}_{\phi}.

This decomposition is the load-bearing object of co-design: neither operator is defined without the other. It is not a specific algorithm but a class of algorithms, indexed by latent space, predictor family, and scoring rule, of which the predictive-sampling systems cited in Section 5.1 are special cases. The two operators run on different clocks: System-1 (ϕ\phi) adapts quickly to realized utilities, while System-2 (θ\theta) improves slowly along the gated gradients. Because better predictions change which interactions are executed, and hence the supervision System-1 receives, one may worry that the coupled loop diverges; two-timescale stochastic approximation (Borkar and Borkar, 2008) gives conditions under which such coupled updates converge, and MPTS trains the two systems jointly in this way in practice (Wang et al., 2026), but a convergence guarantee for the general architecture remains open.

Co-evolution: how the two systems learn together.

Co-evolution concerns how the two systems learn together, (θt,ϕt)→(θt+1,ϕt+1)(\theta_{t},\phi_{t})\to(\theta_{t+1},\phi_{t+1}), as when an agent’s execution harness and the policy running inside it are evolved jointly (Chen et al., 2026), and is dynamical; co-scaling (Section 3.2) concerns how System-1’s optimal capacity responds to System-2’s, and is a comparative-statics problem. As a heuristic reference point for the former, one may expect the predictor’s error to decrease with the amount of executed history and the quality of supervision,

εϕ(t)≲c⁡(θt)|ℋ0:t|,\varepsilon_{\phi}^{(t)}\;\lesssim\;\frac{c(\theta_{t})}{\sqrt{\left|\mathcal{H}_{0:t}\right|}}, (20)

where c⁡(θt)c(\theta_{t}) would decrease as a stronger policy yields cleaner outcomes, and a better predictor in turn makes selection sharper. We write the familiar O(|ℋ0:t|−1/2)O(|\mathcal{H}_{0:t}|^{-1/2}) form, borrowed from independent, identically distributed sampling, only as a benchmark: under adaptive, censored collection the rate need not hold, because the predictor’s training data are gathered by a changing policy and censored by the gate itself (Section 7.2), and a stronger System-2 can make utilities harder rather than easier to predict. Where the loop does work, it resembles self-play along the informativeness axis rather than adversarial reward, and the separation of timescales is what keeps it stable.

Ranking by the posterior mean: using a predictor of given quality.

Let UU be the unknown utility of a candidate and U^\hat{U} the predictor’s output. Intuitively, the predictor should compress history into just enough information about UU: too expressive a predictor wastes parameters and erodes the amortization benefit, while too coarse a predictor cannot discriminate informative from uninformative interactions. An information-bottleneck (IB) objective trades complexity against informativeness,

minq⁡(U^∣ℋ)⁡I⁡(U^,ℋ)⏟predictor complexity−βIB​I⁡(U^,U)⏟prediction informativeness.\min_{q(\hat{U}\mid\mathcal{H})}\;\underbrace{I(\hat{U};\,\mathcal{H})}_{\text{predictor complexity}}\;-\;\beta_{\mathrm{IB}}\,\underbrace{I(\hat{U};\,U)}_{\text{prediction informativeness}}. (21)

Whatever representation U^\hat{U} is learned, the question of how to use it has a clean answer.

Proposition 12 (Rank by the Posterior Mean).

Assume equal costs, a budget of BB executions, and that each candidate’s utility depends on the predictor outputs only through its own, 𝔼⁡[U⁡(i)∣U^]=𝔼⁡[U⁡(i)∣U^​(i)]\mathbb{E}[U(i)\mid\hat{U}]=\mathbb{E}[U(i)\mid\hat{U}(i)]. Then, among all selection rules that see only the predictor outputs U^\hat{U}, executing the BB candidates with the largest posterior mean 𝔼⁡[U∣U^]\mathbb{E}[U\mid\hat{U}] maximizes expected executed utility and hence the IIE. Setting κt\kappa_{t} to the BB-th largest posterior mean makes the admissible set of Eq. (3) exactly that top-BB set, up to ties at the BB-th value.

The proposition is modest: it says nothing about which U^\hat{U} to learn, which is what Eq. (21) addresses. Its practical content is that the calibrated mean of the predictor, not an uncalibrated score, is the right ranking signal.

3.2  Co-Scaling: System-1’s Size as System-2 Grows

Current practice sizes System-2 and treats any selector as an afterthought. Eq. (13) suggests this is incomplete: a larger System-1 lowers its error rates but raises cpredc_{\text{pred}}, and where the balance lies depends on how expensive System-2 is. Let System-1 have a size ss from a totally ordered set 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} (parameters, depth, or context), with error rates fp⁡(s)\mathrm{fp}(s), fn⁡(s)\mathrm{fn}(s) and scoring cost cpred​(s)c_{\text{pred}}(s), and let scaling System-2 multiply every execution cost by a factor k≥1k\geq 1, so that 𝒞¯rel↦k​𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}\mapsto k\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}} and 𝒞¯dead↦k​𝒞¯dead\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}\mapsto k\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}.

Proposition 13 (Co-Scaling Under Fixed Error Curves).

Assume the setting of Proposition 7(ii); that ρu\rho_{u}, fp⁡(s)\mathrm{fp}(s) and fn⁡(s)<1\mathrm{fn}(s)<1 do not depend on kk; that cpred​(s)/(1−fn⁡(s))c_{\text{pred}}(s)/(1-\mathrm{fn}(s)) is non-decreasing in ss; and that the IIE ratio Eq. (13) attains its maximum over 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} for every kk, on a set S⋆​(k)S^{\star}(k) of optimal System-1 sizes. Then (i) S⋆S^{\star} is non-decreasing in kk in the strong set order: if k′>kk^{\prime}>k, s∈S⋆​(k)s\in S^{\star}(k) and s′∈S⋆​(k′)s^{\prime}\in S^{\star}(k^{\prime}), then max⁡(s,s′)∈S⋆​(k′)\max(s,s^{\prime})\in S^{\star}(k^{\prime}) and min⁡(s,s′)∈S⋆​(k)\min(s,s^{\prime})\in S^{\star}(k), so the largest and the smallest optimal sizes, where they exist, are non-decreasing in kk; and (ii) the maximal IIE ratio is non-decreasing in kk.

The mechanism the proof isolates is that scaling System-2 dilutes the predictor’s own cost, cpred/kc_{\text{pred}}/k relative to execution, but not the cost of its mistakes, which grows with System-2 itself, so accuracy becomes relatively cheaper to buy. Under these assumptions, a System-1 that is optimal for one System-2 remains optimal or becomes too small, never too large, as System-2’s cost scale grows; the proposition does not say how large the resulting loss is. The result is comparative statics under fixed error curves: it does not show that growing System-1 helps an evolving executive, nor at what rate System-1 should grow, and both remain experimental hypotheses. Its assumptions do most of the work, and it does not imply the same monotonicity when scaling System-2 changes the prediction problem itself, as happens whenever a stronger executive changes the distribution of utilities, the separation between useful and dead interactions, or the cost structure. The statement is also qualitative: it fixes the direction of co-scaling, not its rate, since fp⁡(s)\mathrm{fp}(s), fn⁡(s)\mathrm{fn}(s) and cpred​(s)c_{\text{pred}}(s) are empirical curves. Measuring them, and hence a compute-optimal ratio between the two systems in the spirit of the parameter-to-data ratio of Hoffmann et al. (2022), is the co-design counterpart of a scaling law (Section 7).

3.3  Example of Architectural Implementation

The decomposition is realized by four domain-agnostic components, summarized by four verbs (See Fig. 6). Represent: candidates {ik}k=1n\{i_{k}\}_{k=1}^{n} are embedded by e:ℐ→ℝdee:\mathcal{I}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}, e.g., frozen language-model encoders in the digital domain; graph or transformer encoders over the structure of the task’s Markov decision process in the physical one. Predict (System-1): a lightweight fϕ:ℝde×ℋ∗→ℝ×ℝ+f_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}\times\mathcal{H}^{*}\to\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{+} outputs (μ^k,σ^k)(\hat{\mu}_{k},\hat{\sigma}_{k}), trained online on executed outcomes, with dϕ≪dθd_{\phi}\ll d_{\theta} keeping cpred≪cexecc_{\text{pred}}\ll c_{\text{exec}}; System-1 may itself be a small language model when semantic understanding is required, but its defining property is computational role rather than model family. Gate: the selection policy πCI\pi_{\mathrm{CI}} produces an execution mask 𝐳t∈{0,1}n\mathbf{z}_{t}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, and when the number executed is set by the threshold rather than fixed, κt\kappa_{t} tracks a target admission rate ρ∗\rho^{*} by stochastic approximation,

κt+1=κt+ακ​(ntadmn−ρ∗),ntadm=|{i:u^ϕ​(i)≥κt}|,\kappa_{t+1}\;=\;\kappa_{t}+\alpha_{\kappa}\!\left(\frac{n_{t}^{\text{adm}}}{n}-\rho^{*}\right),\qquad n_{t}^{\text{adm}}=\bigl|\{i:\hat{u}_{\phi}(i)\geq\kappa_{t}\}\bigr|, (22)

which treats the threshold as a dual variable enforcing that rate; when costs differ, u~ϕ\tilde{u}_{\phi} of Eq. (16) replaces u^ϕ\hat{u}_{\phi} in ntadmn_{t}^{\text{adm}}, and the equal-cost form is shown. Learn: executed interactions are verified, recorded in ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}, and used for one step of 𝒯pred\mathcal{T}_{\text{pred}}, with a decay factor on old history trading stability against tracking non-stationarity. These four components are the operational form of Definition 11, and the ranking rule of Proposition 12 tells the gate how to use the predictor’s output.

Three interfaces of co-design.

Beyond the gate, co-design fixes three interfaces. The knowledge interface determines what is distilled from System-2 into System-1: where System-2 repeatedly solves a class of candidates, the solution itself, not only its value, can be amortized into System-1, as expert iteration does (Anthony et al., 2017), so that System-1 answers routine cases outright and escalates the rest. The representation interface determines what System-1 observes: using System-2’s own features buys accuracy at the price of sharing its blind spots, whereas encoding the candidate independently keeps the two error profiles uncorrelated, and conditioning System-1 on context lets it adapt to a new task, scenario or user without retraining System-2. The feedback interface determines which System-2 outcomes supervise System-1 — realized rewards, gradients, verifier verdicts, or an audit sample of suppressed candidates — and thereby fixes which of its own errors System-1 can ever observe (Section 7.2). Co-design is therefore not merely a size-matching problem. The same position also makes System-1 a natural place for oversight: because it sees every candidate before System-2 acts, cost, irreversibility and safety constraints (Eq. (53)) can be imposed before a capable executive commits.

Gates within gates: hierarchical extensions.

The same gate can operate at several temporal and representational scales at once. For a hierarchy of levels ℓ∈{1,…,Lh}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L_{h}\} (motor, skill, plan), each with its own predictor and threshold,

πCI(ℓ)(it(ℓ)∣ℋ0:t(ℓ))∝exp(βℓu^ϕ(ℓ))[u^ϕ(ℓ)≥κt(ℓ)],\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}^{(\ell)}\!\bigl(i_{t}^{(\ell)}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}^{(\ell)}\bigr)\;\propto\;\exp\!\bigl(\beta_{\ell}\,\hat{u}_{\phi}^{(\ell)}\bigr)\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{u}_{\phi}^{(\ell)}\geq\kappa_{t}^{(\ell)}\right], (23)

with each level gating access to the one below; each πCI(ℓ)\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}^{(\ell)} is normalized over its own admissible set and abstains when that set is empty, as in Definition 1. Analysing the joint dynamics of such a multi-level hierarchy is left open.

4  What Prediction Buys, and Why a Small System-1 Can Work

Sections 2 and 3 defined the gate and the architecture built around it. Co-design pays only if System-1 is both much cheaper than System-2 and accurate enough to steer it; this section asks when both hold. Section 4.1 states the core formal results: what prediction buys, in time and memory, and the regret a cheap predictor risks. The remaining subsections ask why a cheap System-1 can make a useful prediction about an expensive interaction at all, from three complementary views. These connections are interpretive rather than separate contributions; each supplies insight and, under its own assumptions, a guarantee, but none is a derivation of the framework. Information-theoretically (Section 4.2), the quantity gated on is expected information gain net of cost, with epistemic action selection as its limiting case. Generatively (Section 4.3), an interaction is a transition of a world or policy model, and System-1 is an amortized projection of that model onto a single scalar, which is why valuation is cheaper than simulation. Control-theoretically (Section 4.4), executing only what the gate admits is receding-horizon control of a learner whose own dynamics are still being learned.

4.1  Core Results: What Prediction Buys and What It Risks

Predictive sampling has two structural advantages over any scheme that must execute interactions to evaluate them, both following from the fact that u^ϕ\hat{u}_{\phi} scores a candidate from a cheap embedding without performing it: one in time and one, conditionally, in memory. Against them stands one risk, that a cheap predictor selects the wrong interactions, which the end of this subsection bounds.

Screening efficiency.

A reactive filter must execute an interaction before discovering that it was uninformative, paying full cost on the dead fraction. Predictive sampling replaces this with a forward pass of a small model, as in recent predictive prompt and task samplers (Qu et al., 2026a; Mao et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2026a).

Proposition 14 (Screening Gain Relative to Exhaustive Execute-then-Filter Evaluation).

Let a pool of nn candidates contain a fraction ρu\rho_{u} of utility-relevant ones, with execution cost cexecc_{\text{exec}}, screening cost cscreen=cembed+cscorec_{\text{screen}}=c_{\text{embed}}+c_{\text{score}} (encoding the candidate and scoring it; this is the cpredc_{\text{pred}} of Eq. (9)), and r=cscreen/cexecr=c_{\text{screen}}/c_{\text{exec}}. With a perfect screen, acquiring the utility-relevant subset costs

𝒞CI𝒞react=ρu+r\frac{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{CI}}}{\mathcal{C}_{\text{react}}}\;=\;\rho_{u}\;+\;r (24)

of what exhaustive execute-then-filter evaluation spends (𝒞react=n​cexec\mathcal{C}_{\text{react}}=n\,c_{\text{exec}}, the baseline that must execute every candidate to find all relevant ones), a speedup approaching 1/ρu1/\rho_{u} as r→0r\to 0, provided a candidate’s utility class cannot be known without executing or scoring it.

Under the shorthand of Section 4.3 for a dense transformer the costs are concrete: evaluating a pool of nn candidates by rollout to obtain BB utility-relevant ones, versus screening them predictively, costs

𝒞unc\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\text{unc}} =Θ⁡(n​G​L​dmodel2),\displaystyle\;=\;\Theta\!\bigl(n\,G\,L\,d_{\text{model}}^{2}\bigr), (25)
𝒞CI\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{CI}} =Θ⁡(n​cembed)⏟encoding+Θ⁡(n​dϕ2)⏟prediction+Θ⁡(B​G​L​dmodel2)⏟execution,\displaystyle\;=\;\underbrace{\Theta(n\,c_{\text{embed}})}_{\text{encoding}}\;+\;\underbrace{\Theta(n\,d_{\phi}^{2})}_{\text{prediction}}\;+\;\underbrace{\Theta(B\,G\,L\,d_{\text{model}}^{2})}_{\text{execution}}, (26)

with dϕ≪dmodeld_{\phi}\ll d_{\text{model}}, a cost ratio (now including encoding) of B/n+Θ⁡((cembed+dϕ2)/(G​L​dmodel2))B/n+\Theta\bigl((c_{\text{embed}}+d_{\phi}^{2})/(GL\,d_{\text{model}}^{2})\bigr): Eq. (24) with ρu=B/n\rho_{u}=B/n and r=Θ⁡((cembed+dϕ2)/(G​L​dmodel2))r=\Theta\bigl((c_{\text{embed}}+d_{\phi}^{2})/(GL\,d_{\text{model}}^{2})\bigr). Sparse or fused kernels change the constants, not the argument. The encoding term need not be small. A frozen language-model encoder applied to a prompt of length LxL_{x} costs cembed=Θ⁡(Lx​denc2+Lx2​denc)c_{\text{embed}}=\Theta(L_{x}d_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}+L_{x}^{2}d_{\mathrm{enc}}), negligible next to GG rollouts of length LL when Lx​denc2≪G​L​dmodel2L_{x}d_{\mathrm{enc}}^{2}\ll GLd_{\text{model}}^{2} and paid once per candidate when embeddings are cached across the rounds of a static pool; for short rollouts, or when candidates must be re-encoded every round, it can dominate rr. End to end, executing an audit fraction aa of suppressed candidates adds a⁡(1−ρu)a(1-\rho_{u}) to Eq. (24), refitting the predictor adds ctrain/(n​cexec)c_{\text{train}}/(n\,c_{\text{exec}}) per round, and screening errors move the ratio as in Eq. (13); Eq. (24) is the perfect-screen ceiling, not a realized speedup. The error rates separating the realized multiplier from this ceiling are measurable: periodically executing a small audit sample of suppressed candidates estimates fn\mathrm{fn}, and the executed survivors estimate fp\mathrm{fp}; reporting these, and their cost-conditioned versions (Remark 8), turns Eq. (13) into a measured quantity.

Memory scaling.

When evaluation requires real interaction, the candidate pool may also be capped by the memory for in-flight rollouts (KV cache for GG length-LL generations, replay buffers, simulator state). A predictively scored candidate contributes only an embedding e⁡(τ)∈ℝdee(\tau)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}, and embeddings can be streamed.

Proposition 15 (Peak Rollout Memory Under Synchronous Evaluation).

To select the top-BB of nn candidates, synchronous reactive evaluation needs peak memory Mreact​(n)M_{\text{react}}(n), whereas predictive scoring streamed in micro-batches of size bb needs MCI​(n)M_{\mathrm{CI}}(n), where

Mreact​(n)\displaystyle M_{\text{react}}(n) =Θ⁡(n​G​L​dmodel),\displaystyle\;=\;\Theta\!\bigl(n\,G\,L\,d_{\text{model}}\bigr), (27)
MCI​(n)\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{CI}}(n) =Θ⁡(B​G​L​dmodel+b​de+B),\displaystyle\;=\;\Theta\!\bigl(B\,G\,L\,d_{\text{model}}\;+\;b\,d_{e}\;+\;B\bigr), (28)

independent of nn; the pool is then limited only by screening time Θ⁡(n​cpred)\Theta(n\,c_{\text{pred}}) and score storage.

Corollary 16 (Larger Pools Without Rollout Memory).

The best true utility U(1)nU_{(1)}^{n} among nn i.i.d. candidates is non-decreasing in nn: it converges to the essential supremum if utility is bounded, and grows as nξn^{\xi} (in probability, up to a slowly varying factor) if Pr(U>u)=u−1/ξℓ(u)\Pr(U>u)=u^{-1/\xi}\ell(u). Under predictive sampling this gain costs no additional rollout memory (Eq. (28)), provided the predictor ranks the top of the pool correctly.

The memory advantage is conditional on the synchronous premise: a reactive filter that streams executions and keeps only scores also has nn-independent memory, but pays Θ⁡(n​cexec)\Theta(n\,c_{\text{exec}}) time, so the advantage then reduces to the screening gain. More generally, System-1 allocates storage as well as compute — which sample groups stay in a replay buffer, which examples enter a capacity-limited batch (Zou et al., 2025), which demonstrations occupy a context window (Wen et al., 2026b), how much KV cache a request receives — and the rule of Eq. (15) applies unchanged, with memory in place of compute as the cost.

Selection regret.

These savings help only if the cheap predictor selects nearly the right interactions.

Definition 17 (Conditional Regret).

With ℬt∗\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*} the oracle’s top-BB set by true utility ut=u⁡(⋅,θt)u_{t}=u(\cdot;\theta_{t}) in the round-tt pool ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} and ℬ^t\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{t} the set selected by πCI\pi_{\mathrm{CI}} at round tt,

ℛT​(πCI,π∗)=∑t=0T−1[∑i∈ℬt∗ut​(i)−∑i∈ℬ^tut​(i)].\mathcal{R}_{T}(\pi_{\mathrm{CI}},\pi^{*})\;=\;\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\Bigl[\,\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}}u_{t}(i)-\sum_{i\in\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{t}}u_{t}(i)\Bigr]. (29)
Theorem 18 (Regret Bound).

Assume (i) selection is the deterministic limit of the fixed-size batch rule Eq. (47) with μ=0\mu=0 and 𝒜\mathcal{A} the predicted utility u^\hat{u}, the cardinality-constrained form of the master objective Eq. (15), so each round retains the top-BB set by u^\hat{u}; (ii) εϕ=sup0≤t<Tsupi∈ℐt|u^t​(i)−ut​(i)|\varepsilon_{\phi}=\sup_{0\leq t<T}\sup_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}\left|\hat{u}_{t}(i)-u_{t}(i)\right|, a time-uniform error, with u^t(i)=u^ϕt(i∣ℋ0:t)\hat{u}_{t}(i)=\hat{u}_{\phi_{t}}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}); and (iii) gapmin=mint⁡mini∈ℬt∗,j∈ℐt∖ℬt∗⁡(ut​(i)−ut​(j))>0\mathrm{gap}_{\min}=\min_{t}\min_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*},\,j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}}\bigl(u_{t}(i)-u_{t}(j)\bigr)>0. Then

ℛT(πCI,π∗)≤ 2TBεϕ⋅[2εϕ≥gapmin];\mathcal{R}_{T}(\pi_{\mathrm{CI}},\pi^{*})\;\leq\;2\,T\,B\,\varepsilon_{\phi}\,\cdot\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[2\varepsilon_{\phi}\geq\mathrm{gap}_{\min}\right]; (30)

in particular, the selection is exactly the oracle’s whenever 2​εϕ<gapmin2\varepsilon_{\phi}<\mathrm{gap}_{\min}. More generally, with round-specific errors εt=supi∈ℐt|u^t​(i)−ut​(i)|\varepsilon_{t}=\sup_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}\left|\hat{u}_{t}(i)-u_{t}(i)\right| and gaps gapt\mathrm{gap}_{t}, ℛT≤∑t<T2Bεt[2εt≥gapt]\mathcal{R}_{T}\leq\sum_{t<T}2B\varepsilon_{t}\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[2\varepsilon_{t}\geq\mathrm{gap}_{t}\right].

Corollary 19 (High-Probability Regret).

Suppose each round’s pool has at most nn candidates; for every round tt and every candidate outside a blind-spot set 𝒪t⊆ℐt\mathcal{O}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{t} with |𝒪t|≤nood|\mathcal{O}_{t}|\leq n_{\mathrm{ood}}, the error u^t​(i)−ut​(i)\hat{u}_{t}(i)-u_{t}(i) is zero-mean and σϕ\sigma_{\phi}-sub-Gaussian, while errors on 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} are unrestricted; and the utility takes values in an interval of length umaxu_{\max} (e.g. u∈[0,umax]u\in[0,u_{\max}]). Then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta and εϕeff=σϕ​2​ln⁡(2​n​T/δ)\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}=\sigma_{\phi}\sqrt{2\ln(2nT/\delta)},

ℛT(πCI,π∗)≤ 2TBεϕeff[2εϕeff≥gapmin]+Tmin(B,nood)umax.\mathcal{R}_{T}(\pi_{\mathrm{CI}},\pi^{*})\;\leq\;2\,T\,B\,\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[2\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}\geq\mathrm{gap}_{\min}\right]\;+\;T\,\min(B,n_{\mathrm{ood}})\,u_{\max}. (31)

Interpretation. The batch rule of assumption (i) is the cardinality-constrained counterpart of the single-draw greedy limit (Proposition 2), not a consequence of it. For a fixed positive selection margin, regret is exactly zero once the predictor is accurate relative to the separation of interactions (2​εϕ<gapmin2\varepsilon_{\phi}<\mathrm{gap}_{\min}); regret is measured in the units of the declared utility, and gapmin\mathrm{gap}_{\min} enters not as a denominator but as the threshold deciding whether any misranking can occur, with the bound degrading gracefully, linearly in εϕ\varepsilon_{\phi} and BB, once 2​εϕ≥gapmin2\varepsilon_{\phi}\geq\mathrm{gap}_{\min}. In continuous interaction spaces the global gap may vanish, and gapmin\mathrm{gap}_{\min} should then be interpreted as the margin at the BB-th order statistic. The uniform error and strictly positive gap of Theorem 18 are thus the clean idealization that exposes the mechanism; Corollary 19 is the version intended for realistic predictors, and its second term makes explicit that blind spots, not average error, dominate once the predictor is otherwise accurate. The theorem does not imply a self-improving loop: better predictions reduce regret and more informative interactions improve the policy, but a stronger System-2 can make its own utilities harder to predict (Sections 3 and 7.2).

4.2  Understanding Through the Lens of Active Inference

Information net of cost: the utility of an interaction.

Conditional interaction is resource allocation under uncertainty: at each decision point the system chooses whether to spend compute, environment, or inference resources on an interaction whose value is not yet known. Let θ\theta be the latent state of knowledge (model parameters, latent task representations, or beliefs). Executing i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} given history ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t} yields an outcome oo and posterior p⁡(θ∣ℋt,i,o)p(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},i,o). The expected information gain is

𝒰IG(i∣ℋt)=𝔼o∼p⁡(o∣i,ℋt)[DKL[p(θ∣ℋt,i,o)∥p(θ∣ℋt)]]=I(θ;o∣i,ℋt),\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{o\sim p(o\mid i,\mathcal{H}_{t})}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[p(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},i,o)\,\Big\|\,p(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\right]\right]\;=\;I(\theta;o\mid i,\mathcal{H}_{t}), (32)

the utility of Definition 3. Bayesian surprise is the realized, per-outcome divergence measured after execution; expected information gain is its expectation under the predictive distribution, which must be estimated before execution and is what the gate acts on. When outcomes are drawn from the same predictive model, realized surprises on executed interactions are therefore unbiased targets for the pre-execution estimate, which licenses the bootstrapping loop of Section 3. Net of cost,

𝒰⁡(i∣ℋt)=𝒰IG​(i∣ℋt)−λ​𝒞​(i),it∗=arg​maxi∈ℐ⁡𝒰​(i∣ℋt),\mathcal{U}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})=\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})-\lambda\,\mathcal{C}(i),\quad i_{t}^{*}=\argmax_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\;\mathcal{U}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}), (33)

with λ>0\lambda>0 pricing information against resources; this is the β→∞\beta\to\infty limit of Eq. (3) applied to the cost-adjusted score of Eq. (16), rule (b) of Section 2.3, and agrees with the raw-score limit only when costs are equal.

A scalar price treats cost as one-dimensional and fungible, but in deployment latency, money, context occupancy, and safety or irreversibility are not interchangeable and cannot be collapsed into one currency without losing the constraints that matter. The framework accommodates this directly: λ\lambda becomes a vector of prices, κt\kappa_{t} a vector-valued threshold, and the gate a constrained rather than scalar comparison, where a hard deadline or a billing cap weights its component differently from a safety budget. The agentic ledger of Eq. (53) carries exactly these terms; the scalar form is the special case where they share a currency.

Amortized variational estimation of utility.

The exact posterior is unavailable, so a lightweight predictive subsystem (System-1; in the task-sampling literature, a risk prediction model (Wang et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2026a), or a Bayesian filter over a prompt’s solving dynamics (Mao et al., 2026)) maintains a variational approximation qϕ​(θ∣ℋt)q_{\phi}(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}) fitted by minimizing the variational free energy

ℱ(ϕ)=DKL[qϕ(θ∣ℋt)∥p(θ)]−𝔼qϕ[lnp(ℋt∣θ)]=−ELBO(ϕ)≥−lnp(ℋt).\mathcal{F}(\phi)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[q_{\phi}(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\,\Big\|\,p(\theta)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}}\!\bigl[\ln p(\mathcal{H}_{t}\mid\theta)\bigr]=-\mathrm{ELBO}(\phi)\;\geq\;-\ln p(\mathcal{H}_{t}). (34)

Minimizing ℱ\mathcal{F} improves the approximate posterior from which utilities are computed, u^ϕ≈𝒰IG\hat{u}_{\phi}\approx\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}; it does not by itself guarantee better utility estimates or better rankings, since a closer posterior approximation need not order candidates more accurately (compare the remark after Proposition 12). The approximation is substantial: a full Bayesian posterior over a modern network is intractable, so u^ϕ\hat{u}_{\phi} is at best an amortized estimate of Eq. (7), and the gap may be large – that gap is the predictor bottleneck on which every gain of the co-design rests, and Theorem 18 quantifies how it propagates to decisions. In practice the predictor learns the scalar functional directly (Section 4.3) rather than the posterior it summarizes. Unlike a literal free-energy agent, Eq. (34) is not the selection objective (that is Eq. (33)); it only keeps the predictor calibrated.

Epistemic action selection: the active-inference limit.

In active inference an agent minimizes expected free energy (EFE) (Friston, 2010), which has a pragmatic and an epistemic term. Under uniform outcome preferences and with cost handled separately, the expected-free-energy criterion reduces to epistemic action selection based on expected information gain. Conditional interaction adds an explicit pre-execution cost gate and a learned predictor of that quantity.

Proposition 20 (Active-Inference Limit).

Write the expected free energy of interaction ii as

G⁡(i)=−𝔼qϕ​(o∣i)​[ln⁡p⁡(o∣C)]⏟pragmatic value−𝔼qϕ​(o∣i)[DKL[qϕ(θ∣o,i)∥qϕ(θ∣i)]]⏟epistemic value,G(i)=\underbrace{-\,\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(o\mid i)}\!\bigl[\ln p(o\mid C)\bigr]}_{\text{pragmatic value}}-\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(o\mid i)}\!\bigl[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[q_{\phi}(\theta\mid o,i)\,\Big\|\,q_{\phi}(\theta\mid i)\right]\bigr]}_{\text{epistemic value}}, (35)

with preferences p⁡(o∣C)p(o\mid C) over a finite outcome space 𝒪\mathcal{O}. If preferences are uniform and cost is accounted separately through 𝒞⁡(i)\mathcal{C}(i), then

arg​mini∈ℐ⁡G​(i)=arg​maxi∈ℐ⁡Iqϕ​(θ;o∣i)=arg​maxi∈ℐ⁡𝒰IGqϕ​(i∣ℋt),\argmin_{i\in\mathcal{I}}G(i)=\argmax_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\;I_{q_{\phi}}(\theta;o\mid i)=\argmax_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\;\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}^{q_{\phi}}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}), (36)

where 𝒰IGqϕ\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}^{q_{\phi}} is Eq. (32) evaluated under the variational model qϕq_{\phi}, and coincides with 𝒰IG\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}} when qϕq_{\phi} is the exact posterior and predictive. Under non-uniform preferences the two criteria diverge.

The identity is standard active-inference theory and we claim no novelty for it. Expected-free-energy decompositions differ across that literature; we adopt the pragmatic-plus-epistemic form of Eq. (35) and interpret the result as a correspondence, not a foundational derivation: it locates conditional interaction as the cost-gated, predictively amortized special case of epistemic action selection, applicable whenever information gain can be estimated more cheaply than the interaction can be executed.

4.3  Understanding Through the Lens of Decision-Making

Every interaction is coupled to the world through a generative transition kernel

o∼pψ​(o∣i,st),st+1=T⁡(st,i,o),o\;\sim\;p_{\psi}\!\left(o\mid i,\,s_{t}\right),\qquad s_{t+1}\;=\;T\!\left(s_{t},\,i,\,o\right), (37)

where sts_{t} is the state the interaction acts on, oo its outcome, pψp_{\psi} the observation/transition model (environment dynamics in the physical regime; the policy’s own generation in the digital regime), and TT the update folding the outcome into the next state. The uncertain parameter θ\theta and the state sts_{t} may coincide (the policy is both uncertain and evolving) or differ (a robot’s configuration versus its skill parameters).

In the digital regime it is essential to distinguish the interaction, the costly generation of a sequence y=(y1,…,yL)y=(y^{1},\dots,y^{L}) from context xx,

πθ(y∣x)=∏ℓ=1Lπθ(yℓ|x,y<ℓ),\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\;=\;\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\pi_{\theta}\!\left(y^{\ell}\,\middle|\,x,\,y^{<\ell}\right), (38)

which costs LL sequential forward passes (with key–value caching, roughly linear in LL, with a per-token cost set by the model’s depth, width and attention and feed-forward operations; we write Θ⁡(L​dmodel2)\Theta(L\,d_{\mathrm{model}}^{2}) as shorthand, absorbing depth and context-length terms; this is the width-dominated regime L≲dmodelL\lesssim d_{\mathrm{model}}, and with full attention each token also attends over the accumulated context, adding Θ⁡(L2​dmodel)\Theta(L^{2}d_{\mathrm{model}}) per sequence, which key–value caching does not remove), from the outcome, the verdict of a verifier 𝒱\mathcal{V} applied to yy (does the CoT solve the problem, do the unit tests pass):

o=𝒱(y),pψ(o∣i,st)=∑y:𝒱⁡(y)=oπθ(y∣x).o\;=\;\mathcal{V}(y),\qquad p_{\psi}(o\mid i,s_{t})\;=\;\sum_{y\,:\,\mathcal{V}(y)=o}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x). (39)
