The kernel is the generation distribution pushed through the verifier: the verdict oo (often a scalar reward, correct/incorrect, or a score) is what updates the agent’s beliefs, and the tokens yy are merely the costly medium through which it is obtained. The cost is paid on all LL tokens, whereas the information resides in oo, which may be a single bit.

A prompt on which every rollout returns the same verdict yields zero GRPO advantage and hence no group-relative policy-gradient signal despite its full cost. This is a statement about the update, not about belief change: an all-fail group can still inform a posterior over the prompt’s difficulty, and the gradient depends on the sequences through their log-likelihoods, not only on the verdict. The verdict channel models where the cost and the information sit, while the RLVR gate scores the declared proxy uadvu_{\mathrm{adv}} of Remark 9 rather than information gain. The predictor’s task is to forecast the verdict’s declared utility before generating the sequence, which is why cpred≪cexecc_{\mathrm{pred}}\ll c_{\mathrm{exec}}; Fig. 7 shows the pipeline and the point at which System-1 cuts in.

The physical regime is identical with the verifier replaced by the environment’s reward and the sequence by a trajectory with probability ∏kπθ​(ak∣sk)​p​(sk+1∣sk,ak)\prod_{k}\pi_{\theta}(a_{k}\mid s_{k})\,p(s_{k+1}\mid s_{k},a_{k}), whose factors run over physical time steps that cannot be parallelized.

One kernel, two interpretations: dynamics and decision.

Viewed forward in time, Eq. (37) is a dynamical-system transition. Viewed through the agent’s posterior, it defines a decision under uncertainty, since the utility is a functional of pψp_{\psi}:

u(i;ℋt)=𝔼o∼pψ​(o∣i,st)[DKL[p(θ∣ℋt,i,o)∥p(θ∣ℋt)]].u(i;\mathcal{H}_{t})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{o\sim p_{\psi}(o\mid i,s_{t})}\!\Bigl[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[p(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},i,o)\,\Big\|\,p(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{t})\right]\Bigr]. (40)

The gate thus chooses among transitions by the posterior change each is predicted to cause. System-1 is a cheap surrogate estimating Eq. (40) without rolling pψp_{\psi} forward; System-2 is the true transition, paid for only when the surrogate certifies it. Unlike a world model, which learns pψp_{\psi} to simulate outcomes (re-incurring much of the cost the gate avoids), the predictor learns only this scalar functional. The bottleneck is therefore one of valuation, not simulation.

Valuation without simulation: the predictor as a decision-focused surrogate.

This interpretation clarifies what u^ϕ\hat{u}_{\phi} is: an amortized, decision-focused projection of the generative model, enough of pψp_{\psi} to rank transitions by their epistemic value, and no more. That is why the predictor can be small relative to the executive (Proposition 14), and why its failures (Sections 2.4 and 7.2) are failures to value transitions rather than to simulate them. It also motivates the control-theoretic interpretation that follows: once interactions are transitions of a system with a generative model, choosing them to optimize a long-horizon objective is a control problem, and model predictive control is its standard closed-loop solution.

4.4  Understanding Through the Lens of Control Theory

Receding-horizon control of a learning plant.

Conditional interaction is structurally analogous to model predictive control (MPC) of a non-stationary plant whose state is the policy parameter. The analogy is not an equivalence (MPC selects continuous actions; conditional interaction selects subsets of interactions), but it holds component by component.

(1) Model. The plant state is θt\theta_{t}; the predictor Φ\Phi forecasts how an interaction batch ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t} moves it,

θ^t+h=Φh​(θt,ℬt,…),θt+1=θt−η​∇θℒ​(θt,ℬt)+ξt,\hat{\theta}_{t+h}=\Phi_{h}(\theta_{t},\mathcal{B}_{t},\ldots),\qquad\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\eta\,\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t},\mathcal{B}_{t})+\xi_{t}, (41)

where the right-hand equation gives the true dynamics with gradient noise ξt\xi_{t} of covariance ∝|ℬt|−1\propto\left|\mathcal{B}_{t}\right|^{-1}.

(2) Prediction. System-1 forecasts the evaluation risk R⁡(τeval,θ^t+h)R(\tau_{\text{eval}};\hat{\theta}_{t+h}), h=1,…,Hh=1,\dots,H, without executing any interaction (Eq. (46)).

(3) Receding-horizon planning. The control law minimizes discounted predicted risk over admissible batches,

ℬt∗=arg​minℬ⊆𝒟,|ℬ|=B∑h=1Hγh𝔼[R(τeval;θ^t+h)];\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}=\argmin_{\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{D},\,\left|\mathcal{B}\right|=B}\;\sum_{h=1}^{H}\gamma^{h}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[R(\tau_{\text{eval}};\hat{\theta}_{t+h})\right]; (42)

H=1H=1 is a one-step, risk-based analogue of the greedy gate of Eq. (3). It recovers that gate exactly when a candidate’s gross utility is its expected reduction of evaluation risk, costs are equal or priced into the score as in Eq. (16), and the effect of a batch decomposes into candidate-level contributions, while H>1H>1 accounts for how today’s selection shapes tomorrow’s reachable states.

(4) Execution. Only the first batch is executed and the rest re-planned, which makes the loop robust to model error in distant horizons.

(5) Update. Executed outcomes yty_{t} update the model, p(Φ∣ℋ0:t+1)∝p(yt∣ℋ0:t,Φ)p(Φ∣ℋ0:t)p(\Phi\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t+1})\propto p(y_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t},\Phi)\,p(\Phi\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}) (Eq. (45)).

Unlike textbook MPC, plant and controller co-evolve: the state θt\theta_{t} that the controller steers is the same object whose dynamics the model Φ\Phi is still learning. Stability is therefore not classical; it rests on System-1 adapting faster than System-2 (Section 3), and the closed-loop procedure below is this MPC cycle instantiated.

Index policies and optimal stopping.

Define the value of executing ii as

V(i,ℋ0:t)=𝔼[Δ𝒫(i)∣ℋ0:t]−𝒞(i),V(i,\mathcal{H}_{0:t})=\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\Delta\mathcal{P}(i)\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}\bigr]-\mathcal{C}(i), (43)

and execute ii iff V≥V∅V\geq V_{\emptyset}, the value of deferring. Here and in Eq. (52), 𝒞⁡(i)\mathcal{C}(i) is the priced cost, in the units of the utility: λ​𝒞raw​(i)\lambda\,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{raw}}(i) for a scalar ledger, or the composite price of Eq. (53); V∅V_{\emptyset} is on the same scale. Under a discounted, independent-arm bandit approximation with a retirement option, the optimal policy is an index rule: execute while the Gittins index 𝔊(i,ℋ0:t)\mathfrak{G}(i,\mathcal{H}_{0:t}) (Gittins, 1979) exceeds the retirement value κt\kappa_{t},

πCI∗(i)=[𝔊(i,ℋ0:t)≥κt].\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}^{*}(i)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathfrak{G}(i,\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\geq\kappa_{t}\right]. (44)

The Gittins guarantee holds only under those bandit assumptions. Conditional interaction is in general non-stationary (the state θt\theta_{t} drifts) and its interactions are dependent (they share one evolving policy), so Eq. (44) motivates the threshold form of Eq. (3) rather than certifying it. With that qualification, the principle inherits the information-theoretic interpretation of active inference (Proposition 20) and the resource-allocation interpretation of index policies as two limiting analyses, each valid under its own assumptions.

Predict, select, execute, refit: the closed loop.

Fig. 8 shows the resulting pipeline. The MPC components are realized by four operations. Model update: the predictor’s parameters are fitted online by maximizing the conditional log-likelihood of the observed history (the streaming counterpart of Eq. (34)), in practice by a few stochastic gradient steps per round:

maxϕℒML(ϕ):=∑tlnpϕ(ℋt∣ℋ0:t−1).\max_{\phi}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ML}}(\phi)\;:=\;\sum_{t}\ln p_{\phi}\!\bigl(\mathcal{H}_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t-1}\bigr). (45)

Prediction: for each candidate τi\tau_{i}, i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, the predictor returns the predicted mean and uncertainty of the learning signal ℓ\ell,

pϕ(ℓ∣τi,ℋ0:t;θt)⟶{m(ℓi),σ(ℓi)}i=1n,p_{\phi}\!\bigl(\ell\mid\tau_{i},\mathcal{H}_{0:t};\theta_{t}\bigr)\;\longrightarrow\;\bigl\{m(\ell_{i}),\,\sigma(\ell_{i})\bigr\}_{i=1}^{n}, (46)

at a cost independent of the cost of executing τi\tau_{i}, since the predictor operates on embeddings.

Planning and execution: the estimates feed a budgeted subset selection, the fixed-size restriction of Eq. (15),

max⁡∑i=1n𝐳t∈{0,1}n⁡zt(i)​𝒜​(ℓt(i))+μ​𝒮​({τt(i):zt(i)=1}),s.t.​‖𝐳t‖1=B,\max_{\mathbf{z}_{t}\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{t}^{(i)}\,\mathcal{A}(\ell_{t}^{(i)})\;+\;\mu\,\mathcal{S}\!\Bigl(\bigl\{\tau_{t}^{(i)}:z_{t}^{(i)}=1\bigr\}\Bigr),\qquad\text{s.t.}\;\;\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}\right\|_{1}=B, (47)

where 𝒜\mathcal{A} aggregates m⁡(ℓi)m(\ell_{i}) and σ⁡(ℓi)\sigma(\ell_{i}) and 𝒮\mathcal{S} rewards diversity among co-selected interactions. If 𝒜≥0\mathcal{A}\geq 0, μ≥0\mu\geq 0, and 𝒮\mathcal{S} is monotone submodular, the objective is monotone submodular and greedy selection attains a (1−1/e)(1-1/e) approximation. The condition matters: a diversity term that sums pairwise distances, as in Eq. (65), is supermodular, since a new item adds more pairs to a larger set, so the guarantee does not cover it. Monotone submodular choices include facility-location coverage and logdet(I+KS)\log\det(I+K_{S}) for a positive semidefinite similarity kernel KK.

Feedback: executed outcomes are appended to the history,

ℋ0:t+1←ℋ0:t∪{(τt(i),ℓt(i)):zt(i)=1},\mathcal{H}_{0:t+1}\;\leftarrow\;\mathcal{H}_{0:t}\,\cup\,\Bigl\{\bigl(\tau_{t}^{(i)},\,\ell_{t}^{(i)}\bigr)\,:\,z_{t}^{(i)}=1\Bigr\}, (48)

and fed back into Eq. (45) on the next round. The update is asymmetric: only executed interactions enter ℋ\mathcal{H}, so the predictor is trained on a biased sample of its own choosing, and the validity of the procedure rests on the timescale separation discussed in Section 3; the statistical consequences of this censoring are discussed in Section 7.2. Together, the four operations realize a complete closed-loop instance of the principle in which the predictive subsystem and the executive policy co-adapt through their shared history. Model predictive task sampling and its in-context extension run this loop over tasks (Wang et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2026a), and recent agentic RL methods carry it inside long-horizon trajectories, allocating rollouts to shared prefixes and propagating terminal rewards back through the resulting trees (Zou et al., 2026b; Zou et al., 2026a).

5  Conditional Interaction Across Digital and Physical Domains

Reasoning-model fine-tuning and embodied-agent training are instances of one abstraction, distinguished by state space, cost structure, and verifier. In both, conditional interaction learns a predictor of value from past outcomes and executes the interactions whose predicted value clears the threshold κt\kappa_{t} of Definition 1. The two instantiations share one predicament — finding out whether a task is worth training on often costs almost as much as training on it — while differing in why. Table 1 summarizes the correspondence together with the test-time and agentic settings.

5.1  Digital and Physical Instantiations in the Literature

Digital: from filtering after generation to predicting before it.

In RLVR only prompts whose sampled responses disagree carry a group-relative advantage, and that band drifts as the policy improves (Qu et al., 2026b). Early methods filter after generating: dynamic sampling in DAPO discards prompts whose groups are uniformly correct or wrong (Yu et al., 2026), and online difficulty filtering keeps prompts of intermediate pass rate (Bae et al., 2026), both paying in full for the rollouts that reveal a prompt to be uninformative — the execute-then-filter baseline of Proposition 14. Later methods predict before generating: GRESO skips prompts that their reward history marks as likely zero-variance (Zheng et al., 2026); MoPPS tracks each prompt’s success rate with an online Bayesian posterior and approaches an evaluation-intensive dynamic-sampling baseline with far fewer rollouts (Qu et al., 2026a); DPS, BOTS and PCL model prompt difficulty with a hidden-Markov process, Thompson sampling and an on-policy value model, respectively (Mao et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026); and GPS trains one small generative predictor on the shared optimization history to select prompts for a much larger reasoning model, improving training efficiency and test-time compute allocation (Qu et al., 2026c). The same move extends beyond prompts, to online batch selection in supervised fine-tuning (Zou et al., 2025), to demonstration selection for in-context learning, where a small trained model makes a single edit to the retrieved demonstrations instead of iteratively scoring or searching over demonstration subsets (Wen et al., 2026b), to rollout allocation across tasks and trajectory prefixes in agentic RL (Zou et al., 2026b), and to critic-free, tree-aware credit assignment for long-horizon agents (Zou et al., 2026a). These results illustrate rather than validate the framework.

Physical: from randomizing to predicting adaptation risk.

For embodied agents, judging a task configuration means acting on it, on hardware or in a high-fidelity simulator, at the pace of physics. Domain randomization trains across wide ranges of simulated appearance and dynamics (Tobin et al., 2017), with an explicit assessment of transfer (Muratore et al., 2018); because uniform randomization spends most trajectories on mastered configurations, later work prioritizes, through active and automatic domain randomization (Mehta et al., 2020; Akkaya et al., 2019) and through environment design and level replay driven by regret or learning potential (Dennis et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021), though still by executing configurations to score them. When robustness matters, the target is the adverse tail of post-adaptation risk, measured by the conditional value-at-risk (Rockafellar et al., 2000) and pursued in robust meta-learning (Finn et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2023; Lv et al., 2024), risk-averse planning (Carpin et al., 2016) and safety-critical scenario generation (Rempe et al., 2022). Locating that tail requires evaluating many tasks; MPTS removes the evaluation by learning a risk predictive model from the optimization history (Wang et al., 2026), and its successors add posterior sampling and diversity (Qu et al., 2025) and in-context risk prediction (Wen et al., 2026a), yielding curriculum-like sampling under a calibrated predictor.

What the two literatures share.

Evaluation requires generating in the digital regime and acting in the physical one, yet both literatures converge on the same loop: System-1 scores a candidate from cheap features and history, System-2 executes only what clears the score, and System-2’s outcomes refit System-1. They differ in utility (mixed outcomes versus tail adaptation risk; Remark 5) and in the conserved resource (compute versus actuation); their acquisition functions are collected in Appendix B. Unlike post-hoc data valuation by influence functions or data Shapley (Koh and Liang, 2017; Ghorbani and Zou, 2019), and unlike active learning, experimental design and bandit index policies over a static pool (Krishnakumar, 2007; Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995; Gittins, 1979), these methods value candidates before execution and track a moving learner. They also extend earlier fast–slow pairings, such as expert iteration and AlphaZero (Anthony et al., 2017; Silver et al., 2018) and speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), from one game or one decoding step to training and deployment.

6  Conditional Interaction at Test Time

The framework so far concerns training. The same decision problem appears at inference, but with a different state, utility and cost ledger. Nothing in Definition 1 and Eq. (9) requires the training setting: the rule gates an interaction on predicted utility net of cost, whether the resource is a training rollout or an inference-time forward pass. We argue that test-time scaling and adaptive decision-making, usually studied separately, can be cast as test-time instances of conditional interaction. Prospective metacognitive control of test-time compute is an active line of work in its own right (Nazi and Dipta, 2026; Cao et al., 2026); the contribution here is not to discover it but to place it in the same ledger as training. Co-design therefore does not end at deployment: the System-1 that shaped training goes on to ration System-2’s inference effort.

At deployment θ\theta is fixed; what varies, and costs, is the computation and the number of real-world actions spent per output. An interaction is now an increment of inference: a reasoning step, an extra sample, a tool or retrieval call, or a physical action. The executive state is bt=p(a∣q,ℋ0:t)b_{t}=p(a\mid q,\mathcal{H}_{0:t}), a predictive distribution over candidate answers or latent solution states aa for query qq, which we call the belief state for convenience without requiring a literal Bayesian posterior. The utility of an increment is

𝕀tt(it)=𝔼[DKL[bt+1∥bt]|ℋ0:t,it],\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{tt}}(i_{t})\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[b_{t+1}\,\Big\|\,b_{t}\right]\;\big|\;\mathcal{H}_{0:t},\,i_{t}\,\bigr], (49)

and its cost is the inference compute or actuation it requires, so Definition 1 applies verbatim with u^ϕ\hat{u}_{\phi} predicting Eq. (49) and κt\kappa_{t} as a stopping threshold. Eq. (49) measures epistemic movement, not improvement: a changed answer is not necessarily a better one, so movement of btb_{t} should be interpreted as computational sensitivity, and accuracy must be checked separately. The test-time hypothesis is that this sensitivity predicts where additional computation is useful. Only the ledger changes — parameter belief change becomes answer belief change, and training compute becomes inference compute — and that substitution is the entire test-time claim.

6.1  Face I: Efficient Test-Time Scaling

Test-time scaling improves a fixed model by spending more inference per query (longer CoT, repeated sampling with aggregation, tree search, tool calls). This spend is highly heterogeneous across queries: easy ones are solved by the first short trajectory and the hardest by no feasible budget, so extra reasoning moves btb_{t} only in an intermediate band, the analogue of the partially solved prompts of Section 5.1. Uniform test-time scaling therefore inherits the vanishing marginal efficiency of Eq. (1), now in inference cost. Conditional interaction continues to spend only while the predicted change of increment ctc_{t} clears the threshold:

halt at step t⋆=min{t:u^ϕ(ct∣ℋ0:t)<κt},\text{halt at step }t^{\star}\;=\;\min\bigl\{\,t:\hat{u}_{\phi}(c_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})<\kappa_{t}\,\bigr\}, (50)

the optimal-stopping form of Eqs. (43) and (44) applied at inference. Familiar techniques are choices of increment and predictor: adaptive-length reasoning and early exit gate one more decoding step, adaptive self-consistency one more sample, budget-aware tree search one more node expansion. All suppress increments predicted to leave btb_{t} unchanged, so one proposition covers them, with one caveat. Eq. (49) values the next increment, and an increment can leave btb_{t} unchanged while enabling later ones that do change it, as when an intermediate thought pays off only several steps on. A gate that halts on the next-step utility can therefore stop before such a delayed gain. The guarantee below is stated for the continuation utility

ucont(q)=𝔼[DKL[bC∥b1]|q,ℋ0:1],u_{\mathrm{cont}}(q)\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[b_{C}\,\Big\|\,b_{1}\right]\;\big|\;q,\mathcal{H}_{0:1}\,\bigr], (51)

the expected belief change from the first increment to the full budget CC, which System-1 must predict after the probing increment and whose prediction cost is charged as cpredc_{\text{pred}}. Predicting the value of the next token, of a whole continuation, and of the final answer are different tasks, and the second and third are generally harder. Eq. (50) with the next-step utility is covered only under a no-delayed-gain condition: a query whose next increment leaves btb_{t} unchanged in expectation gains nothing from any later increment. Two stopping policies must also be kept apart. The one-probe gate spends one increment, predicts Eq. (51), and then stops or runs to the full budget; it is the policy Proposition 22 covers. A sequential halting policy, Eq. (50), re-decides at every step and should score the continuation value from the current state, ucont,t(q)=𝔼[DKL[bC∥bt]∣q,ℋ0:t]u_{\mathrm{cont},t}(q)=\mathbb{E}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[b_{C}\,\Big\|\,b_{t}\right]\mid q,\mathcal{H}_{0:t}]; a halt at step tt then loses accuracy only on a false negative, so by a union bound its accuracy loss is at most ∑tδFN,t\sum_{t}\delta_{\mathrm{FN},t}, the sum of the per-step false-negative masses, and its cost must charge a prediction at every step. We do not develop that guarantee further. Its error term, and that of Proposition 23, rests on the following margin condition, which turns a score error into a misclassification rate.

Lemma 21 (Misclassification Under a Margin Condition).

Let candidates i∼𝒟i\sim\mathcal{D} be utility-relevant when u⁡(i)≥uminu(i)\geq u_{\min}, let the gate admit ii when u^​(i)≥umin\hat{u}(i)\geq u_{\min}, and suppose |u^​(i)−u⁡(i)|≤ε\left|\hat{u}(i)-u(i)\right|\leq\varepsilon for every ii. More generally, let the gate admit ii when u^​(i)≥κ\hat{u}(i)\geq\kappa. Every misclassified candidate, admitted while dead or suppressed while relevant, then lies in the band ℬε={i:κ−ε≤u⁡(i)<umin}∪{i:umin≤u⁡(i)<κ+ε}\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}=\{i:\kappa-\varepsilon\leq u(i)<u_{\min}\}\cup\{i:u_{\min}\leq u(i)<\kappa+\varepsilon\}, so the misclassified masses satisfy δFP+δFN≤Pri∼𝒟⁡(ℬε)\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}+\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}\leq\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}). With κ=umin\kappa=u_{\min}, if the true utility satisfies the margin condition Pri∼𝒟⁡(|u⁡(i)−umin|≤ε)≤m​ε\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}}\bigl(\left|u(i)-u_{\min}\right|\leq\varepsilon\bigr)\leq m\,\varepsilon with constant mm, then the gate misclassifies, by admitting a dead candidate or suppressing a relevant one, at most a fraction m​εm\,\varepsilon of candidates.

A density of uu bounded by m/2m/2 on [umin−ε,umin+ε][u_{\min}-\varepsilon,u_{\min}+\varepsilon] gives the condition. The band, not the margin condition, is the general object, and atoms are the case that matters in practice. At test time many queries have continuation utility exactly zero, and relevance means u>0u>0 (umin→0+u_{\min}\to 0^{+}); the whole atom then lies within ε\varepsilon of the floor, and the margin condition with κ=umin\kappa=u_{\min} fails. Placing the gate threshold above the error, κ>ε\kappa>\varepsilon, excludes the atom: a query with u=0u=0 has u^≤ε<κ\hat{u}\leq\varepsilon<\kappa and is never admitted, so δFP=0\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}=0 and δFN≤Pr⁡(0<u<κ+ε)\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}\leq\Pr(0<u<\kappa+\varepsilon), the mass of small but nonzero utilities. Whether that mass is small is a property of the task distribution, to be measured on an audit pool, not an assumption to take for granted.

Proposition 22 (Conditional Test-Time Cost Bound Under a Halting Margin).

Let 𝒜tt\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tt}} be the queries on which the full budget is more accurate in expectation than one increment, with density ρacctt\rho_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\mathrm{tt}}, and let the gate threshold a declared test-time utility whose relevant set contains 𝒜tt\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tt}}, with density ρutt≥ρacctt\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}}\geq\rho_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\mathrm{tt}}. Let unconditional scaling spend CC unit increments per query, let the answer be a function of the belief state, and let the selection policy be the one-probe gate: it spends one probing increment plus cpredc_{\text{pred}} and then halts or continues to the full budget, with δFN\delta_{\mathrm{FN}} and δFP\delta_{\mathrm{FP}} the fractions of all queries that are relevant but halted and dead but continued. Then the gated policy loses at most δFN\delta_{\mathrm{FN}} accuracy while spending at most a fraction

ρutt+1+cpredC+δFP\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}}+\frac{1+c_{\text{pred}}}{C}+\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}

of the unconditional compute, a multiplier approaching 1/ρutt1/\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}} as C→∞C\to\infty and δFP→0\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}\to 0. By Lemma 21, δFN+δFP≤Pr⁡(ℬεϕ)\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}+\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}\leq\Pr(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon_{\phi}}) for a predictor with error at most εϕ\varepsilon_{\phi}, which is at most m​εϕm\varepsilon_{\phi} under the margin condition. The tightest choice is the accuracy-gain utility itself, for which ρutt=ρacctt\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}}=\rho_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\mathrm{tt}}. The continuation utility of Eq. (51) with umin→0+u_{\min}\to 0^{+} is also admissible: if its value is zero then bC=b1b_{C}=b_{1} almost surely, so the answer, and with it the accuracy, is unchanged; its gate should use κ>εϕ\kappa>\varepsilon_{\phi}, so that the atom of zero-utility queries is never admitted. With density ρconttt≥ρacctt\rho_{\mathrm{cont}}^{\mathrm{tt}}\geq\rho_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\mathrm{tt}} it gives the weaker multiplier 1/ρconttt1/\rho_{\mathrm{cont}}^{\mathrm{tt}}. The next-step utility of Eq. (49) is admissible only under the no-delayed-gain condition.

The proposition is the inference-time counterpart of Eq. (12), with the per-query halting decision in place of per-batch selection, and only ρutt\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}} has to be re-estimated. Its status needs care: the multiplier follows given a small informative fraction and an accurate halting predictor, and unlike the training side neither premise has been measured, making this the one place where our efficiency claims lack even indirect support. The falsification protocol is direct: measure ρacctt\rho_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\mathrm{tt}} as the fraction of queries whose answer becomes correct when the budget is raised from a short default to the full one, run unconditional scaling at full budget for reference accuracy, then run the one-probe gate and record accuracy and mean compute. A larger accuracy loss than the false-negative mass δFN\delta_{\mathrm{FN}} measured on an audit sample, or a failure to realize the saving, refutes the test-time claim.

6.2  Face II: Efficient Adaptive Decision-Making

For systems acting in the world, the increments are external actions (a manipulation, a sensor query, a tool call, a clarifying question), each with a real cost and the capacity to change beliefs. The efficient policy acts when predicted value of information net of cost is positive, i.e. Eq. (43) promoted to an online rule:

execute it⟺𝔼[Δ𝒫(it)∣ℋ0:t]−𝒞(it)≥V∅,\text{execute }i_{t}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[\Delta\mathcal{P}(i_{t})\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}\bigr]\;-\;\mathcal{C}(i_{t})\;\geq\;V_{\emptyset}, (52)

with Δ​𝒫​(it)\Delta\mathcal{P}(i_{t}) the expected improvement in task return, 𝒞⁡(it)\mathcal{C}(i_{t}) the priced cost defined after Eq. (43), and V∅V_{\emptyset} the value of deferring or taking the cheap default, adapted online as in Eq. (22). Reducing task uncertainty is a different utility, not a second reading of Δ​𝒫\Delta\mathcal{P}: it instantiates the same rule with Δ​𝒫\Delta\mathcal{P} replaced by the expected entropy reduction of the task posterior. Selective tool use, active perception, and interrupt-or-defer control are Eq. (52) with different iti_{t} and utilities: a tool call scored by answer-entropy reduction, a sensor movement or question scored by world-model belief change, a re-plan triggered when predicted plan value degrades. The adaptation-risk predictor that prioritized training tasks in Section 5.1 becomes, at deployment, the value-of-information predictor that gates actions: efficient adaptive decision-making can be cast as conditional interaction with the world as the executive.

6.3  Selective Agentic Tool and Computer Use

An agent that plans, retrieves, calls tools, asks questions and operates a computer faces Eq. (52) against a composite cost. At step tt it holds an answer/plan belief state btb_{t} and chooses from a heterogeneous menu (think, retrieve or call a tool, ask, delegate, commit), each action costing

𝒞⁡(it)=λ⊤​c​(it)+λrisk​Pr⁡[irrecoverable∣it],\mathcal{C}(i_{t})\;=\;\lambda^{\top}c(i_{t})\;+\;\lambda_{\mathrm{risk}}\,\Pr[\text{irrecoverable}\mid i_{t}], (53)

where c⁡(it)=(clat​(it),c$​(it),ctok​(it))c(i_{t})=\bigl(c_{\text{lat}}(i_{t}),\,c_{\$}(i_{t}),\,c_{\text{tok}}(i_{t})\bigr) collects latency, metered spend and context tokens, λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 prices them, and λrisk\lambda_{\mathrm{risk}} prices an irrecoverable side effect. In the co-designed pair, System-1 (typically a verifier head or small router) admits iti_{t} only when Eq. (52) holds for this cost, with V∅V_{\emptyset} the value of committing the current best answer, and System-2 is the agent that executes it. Tool use and computer use differ only in the size of the space to search: a tool call is one typed request among a few, whereas a computer-use episode branches at each of tens of steps, every one costing a screenshot, a model call and unparallelizable time.

Proposition 23 (Conditional Agentic Cost Bound for Separable Actions).

Suppose (a) omitting any set of decision-irrelevant actions leaves the answer unchanged; (b) the gate thresholds a predicted relevance score with error at most εϕ\varepsilon_{\phi}, and on every task the action scores satisfy the margin condition of Lemma 21 with constant mm, so that in expectation at most a fraction m​εϕm\,\varepsilon_{\phi} of the actions are misclassified; and (c) prediction costs a fraction rr of an average action. Consider tasks with NN candidate actions in which no action costs more than RcR_{c} times the task’s average action cost. If utility-relevant actions carry a share ρu𝒞\rho_{u}^{\mathcal{C}} of the expected call-everything cost (the cost-weighted density of utility-relevant actions, which reduces to their fraction ρu\rho_{u} when all actions cost the same), the conditional agent’s accuracy is within N​m​εϕNm\,\varepsilon_{\phi} of call-everything accuracy, at expected cost

𝔼⁡[𝒞CI]≤(ρu𝒞+r+m​εϕ​Rc)​𝔼​[𝒞all].\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{CI}}]\;\leq\;\bigl(\rho_{u}^{\mathcal{C}}+r+m\,\varepsilon_{\phi}\,R_{c}\bigr)\,\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{C}_{\text{all}}].

The proposition is therefore a separable-action special case. Assumption (a) fails on long interface trajectories, where a dozen individually uninformative clicks may be jointly needed to reach the screen that matters, and whenever a locally uninformative action, such as navigating, authenticating or opening a file, is a prerequisite for a useful one; there utility belongs to the sub-trajectory or state transition, valued by a state-dependent value of information, and the unit to score is a sub-trajectory, and since the accuracy loss grows linearly in NN, the per-action error must shrink with the horizon. Pure exploration (Section 2.4) and mandated actions such as safety logging lie outside the gate. Across Sections 6.1 and 6.2 and this subsection the predict–gate–execute pattern is shared while utilities and costs are not (Table 1), so a System-1 calibrated against System-2 during training can serve as the inference-time router, with deployment outcomes flowing back as its training data.

7  A Testable Scaling Hypothesis, and Open Problems

Co-design makes two kinds of prediction: what the pair should achieve as it scales, and where it can fail. We state the first as a testable hypothesis about informative compute, then turn to the main obstacle — System-1 is supervised only by the interactions it lets System-2 execute — and to open problems. It helps to separate three kinds of claim. Proved under stated assumptions: the IIE accounting (Proposition 7), the screening and memory results (Propositions 14 and 15), the regret bounds (Theorems 18 and 19), the test-time and agentic cost bounds (Propositions 22 and 23), co-scaling under fixed error curves (Proposition 13) and horizontal rescaling (Proposition 24). Supported by application-specific evidence: the savings of predictive prompt and task sampling (Section 5.1). Proposed hypotheses: a co-designed frontier that dominates on cost, quality of service and task success at once (Fig. 3), the decay of ρu\rho_{u} (Hypothesis 25), and a changed scaling exponent.

7.1  The Scaling Hypothesis: Informative Compute

Standard scaling laws express loss as a power law in total compute, ℒ⁡(𝒞)=(𝒞0/𝒞)αC\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{C})=(\mathcal{C}_{0}/\mathcal{C})^{\alpha_{C}}, with

𝒞info​(𝒞)=∫0𝒞ρuexec​(c)​𝑑c\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{info}}(\mathcal{C})\;=\;\int_{0}^{\mathcal{C}}\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{exec}}(c)\,dc (54)

the informative compute absorbed along a run, where ρuexec​(c)\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{exec}}(c) is the executed fraction at cumulative compute cc, the share of compute then spent on utility-relevant interactions. Under unconditional training it equals the cost-weighted pool density

ρu𝒞​(θc)=𝔼i∼𝒟[𝒞(i)[u(i;θc)≥umin]]𝔼i∼𝒟​[𝒞​(i)],\rho_{u}^{\mathcal{C}}(\theta_{c})\;=\;\frac{\mathbb{E}_{i\sim\mathcal{D}}\bigl[\mathcal{C}(i)\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[u(i;\theta_{c})\geq u_{\min}\right]\bigr]}{\mathbb{E}_{i\sim\mathcal{D}}[\mathcal{C}(i)]}, (55)

the compute share of relevant interactions, as in Proposition 23; it reduces to the interaction share ρu​(θc)\rho_{u}(\theta_{c}) only when execution costs are equal, and can differ substantially otherwise. Under a perfect gate it is one. With equal costs, as Proposition 24 assumes, the two runs of Proposition 24 accumulate informative compute at rates ρu\rho_{u} and 11. The scaling hypothesis below is stated for ρu\rho_{u} in this equal-cost case; with heterogeneous costs, ρu𝒞\rho_{u}^{\mathcal{C}} takes its place. The framework predicts more than a constant-factor gain: if the fraction of utility-relevant interactions changes as a learner becomes more capable, total compute is not the only meaningful coordinate of scaling, and the question is whether performance curves become more comparable when plotted against Eq. (54). Two hypotheses answer differently and are experimentally distinguishable: the conservative one is that gating produces only a horizontal rescaling, the stronger one that it also alters the trajectory of interaction density and thereby the effective exponent.

Proposition 24 (Horizontal Rescaling of the Scaling Curve).

Suppose (a) unconditional training follows a loss curve ℒbase​(𝒞)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathcal{C}) on a pool whose density of utility-relevant interactions is a constant ρu∈(0,1]\rho_{u}\in(0,1]; (b) dead interactions leave the learner unchanged; (c) progress depends only on the utility-relevant interactions executed, whose distribution and order the selection policy preserves; and (d) the selection policy is perfect, prediction is free, and executions cost the same. Then

ℒCI​(𝒞)=ℒbase​(𝒞/ρu),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CI}}(\mathcal{C})\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}\!\left(\mathcal{C}/\rho_{u}\right), (56)

i.e. on a log-compute axis the conditional curve is the unconditional one shifted left by ln⁡(1/ρu)\ln(1/\rho_{u}).

This is a rescaling identity, valid for any shape of ℒbase\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}: it is the precise content of the 1/ρu1/\rho_{u} multiplier used throughout. Assumption (a) fixes ρu\rho_{u}, which the next hypothesis denies in general; when the pool fraction drifts, the constant factor becomes the time-varying reparameterization Eq. (54), and that integral is what the curve-collapse test below plots against.

Hypothesis 25 (Informative Interaction Decay).

After an initial transient, ρu​(θt)\rho_{u}(\theta_{t}) is non-increasing as the system improves: mastered interactions leave the utility-relevant set, so ρu\rho_{u} tracks the shrinking measure of reachable but not-yet-mastered interactions.

The hypothesis is empirical and can fail, since new capabilities can expose new informative tasks and an improved predictor changes what is selected. Its logical direction matters, and it rests on an assumption that the definition of ρu\rho_{u} does not supply. Nothing in Eq. (14) makes relevant interactions equally useful: two prompts with non-zero advantage can produce updates of very different size and direction. We therefore assume constant conditional progress: over the regime studied, a unit of utility-relevant compute reduces the expected loss by the same amount η\eta. Under that assumption unconditional learning is the absorption of informative compute, d​ℒ/d​𝒞=−η​ρu​(θ)d\mathcal{L}/d\mathcal{C}=-\eta\,\rho_{u}(\theta), and an observed power law corresponds to one particular decay, ρu=k​ℒ1+1/α\rho_{u}=k\,\mathcal{L}^{1+1/\alpha} with αC=α\alpha_{C}=\alpha, but it does not follow that ρu\rho_{u} produces the scaling law. The construction establishes consistency, not derivation: an independently measured trajectory must satisfy it, so slower decay means a larger exponent. Gradient noise, intrinsic dimension and loss curvature generate power-law-like curves too; ρu\rho_{u} is simply the most actionable, since gating intervenes on it directly (Remark 9).

Against informative compute measured as in Eq. (14), the null implied by Proposition 24 predicts that the two curves coincide, the alternative that the gated curve is steeper even after rescaling. A strict improvement would not by itself establish Hypothesis 25, since different optimizer dynamics, lower gradient variance, a selection-induced curriculum or reduced redundancy could all produce it; attributing it to ρu\rho_{u} requires measuring ρu\rho_{u} along both runs and testing whether the difference in exponents is explained by the difference in those trajectories. The savings reported in Section 5.1 are consistent with the null.

7.2  Selective Supervision: The Gate Censors Its Own Training Data

The most consequential technical limitation is structural: once System-1 decides which interactions are executed, it also decides which interactions it is trained on. With pcand​(i)p_{\mathrm{cand}}(i) the candidate distribution and e(i)=Pr[i executed∣i,ℋ0:t]e(i)=\Pr[i\text{ executed}\mid i,\mathcal{H}_{0:t}] the gate’s execution probability, the predictor is trained on

ptrain​(i)∝pcand​(i)​e​(i)≠pcand​(i),p_{\mathrm{train}}(i)\;\propto\;p_{\mathrm{cand}}(i)\,e(i)\;\neq\;p_{\mathrm{cand}}(i), (57)

so labels are missing not at random: whether an outcome is observed depends on the predictor’s own estimate of it, and in the worst case a candidate scored as low-value is suppressed, its outcome never observed, and the score never corrected. This is the selective-labels problem of algorithmic decision-making (Lakkaraju et al., 2017), the positivity problem of causal inference, and, under shifting distributions, the label-querying problem of active self-training (Zhou et al., 2022b; Zhou et al., 2022a). Three features make it tractable rather than hopeless. Positivity can be designed in, but not by temperature: the indicator in Eq. (3) gives every candidate with u^<κt\hat{u}<\kappa_{t} probability zero at every finite β\beta, so a soft gate only randomizes within the admissible set. Positivity needs an explicit component that reaches the suppressed region: an exploration mixture πϵ=(1−ϵ)​πCI+ϵ​π0\pi_{\epsilon}=(1-\epsilon)\,\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}+\epsilon\,\pi_{0} with π0​(i)>0\pi_{0}(i)>0 on the whole pool, which gives e⁡(i)≥ϵ​π0​(i)e(i)\geq\epsilon\,\pi_{0}(i) per draw, or independent audit sampling of suppressed candidates at a known rate aa, which gives e⁡(i)≥ae(i)\geq a. Either way e⁡(i)≥emin>0e(i)\geq e_{\min}>0. The propensities are known, because the gate assigns them, so weighting the predictor’s loss by 1/e⁡(i)1/e(i) (Horvitz and Thompson, 1952), or combining that weighting with the predictor’s own regression in a doubly robust estimator (Dudík et al., 2011), gives unbiased estimates of its error on the full candidate distribution. And the audit sample of suppressed candidates (Section 4.1) is exactly such a positivity-preserving exploration stream, provided its rate is fixed independently of the predictor’s scores. What remains open is quantitative: how large emine_{\min} must be for the predictor’s error to shrink while the policy and the candidate distribution drift, how the variance of inverse-propensity weights trades against the screening gain, and whether any rate like Eq. (20) survives adaptive, censored collection. Of all the problems the framework raises, we regard this as the one most in need of theory.

7.3  Open Problems and Outlook

The decay profile of ρu​(θt)\rho_{u}(\theta_{t}) has not yet been measured, and doing so is the cleanest single test of the framework; it would also test a mechanistic account of emergence, since a sub-skill whose ρu\rho_{u} crosses a usable threshold abruptly should appear abruptly. We regard this as the most actionable contribution of this Perspective.

Several questions stay open. Because aggressive gating discards informative interactions while permissive gating readmits dead ones, efficiency is maximized at an interior admission rate ρ∗​(εϕ)\rho^{*}(\varepsilon_{\phi}), whose characterization sits inside a non-stationary bandit problem (Auer et al., 2002), as does its inference-time counterpart, whether a halting predictor can reach the accuracy Proposition 22 requires without its own forward pass eroding the savings. Proposition 13 fixes the direction in which System-1 should grow with System-2, and sweeping System-1’s size at several System-2 sizes while measuring fp\mathrm{fp}, fn\mathrm{fn} and cpredc_{\text{pred}} would give the compute-optimal split between them. And the framework is single-learner: in agent societies, self-play and debate, informativeness is a property of joint beliefs, suggesting a relational utility and an informative fraction defined on an interaction graph, since an interaction uninformative to its initiator may inform an observer. We regard this last as the most consequential boundary of the framework.

Conditional interaction finally resonates, without being equivalent, with the enactive view of cognition urged for AI by Rafiee and Sutton (2026), building on Varela et al. (2017) and the “era of experience” (Silver and Sutton, 2025): perception as selective activity, in which an agent acts in order to reveal information. Our utility nonetheless answers to an externally given task and cost ledger rather than the agent’s own self-maintenance, so we formalize the selective-engagement facet alone. Within that scope, routing tasks to System-2 executives (Section 2.3) extends the gate from data to model selection and Section 6 adds the inference boundary, so a fully conditional system, whose data, computation, inference effort and external actions are all gated by a co-designed System-1, is a promising architecture for resource-efficient intelligence at scale, and the argument strengthens with capability if both Hypothesis 25 and Proposition 13 hold. Beyond human-level performance (Mulgan, 2016), human data and curricula would no longer say what is worth learning, and a system would have to choose its own experiments; its System-1 would then decide what a superhuman System-2 learns and does, making the gate a major source of efficiency.

8  Conclusion

This work poses the perspective that the next stage of progress toward AGI may come from the co-design of System-1 and System-2: a cheap System-1 that values each candidate interaction before it is paid for, and a costly System-2 that executes only what clears the gate, each trained on the other’s outputs. Conditional interaction, the predict–gate–execute–update loop that couples them, applies alike to training rollouts, test-time reasoning and agentic actions, and under explicit assumptions yields screening, memory, regret and co-scaling results. These results motivate the scaling hypothesis of Section 7. Our answer to the research question is therefore a qualified yes: the co-design is promising wherever interactions are costly, unequal in value and predictable in advance. The decisive next step is measurement: quantify ρu\rho_{u}, compare scaling curves at matched informative compute, and test whether co-design changes more than a constant factor.

Appendix A Proofs

Each subsection below restates a result exactly as it appears in the main text, keeping its original number, and proves it step by step. All results are proved for a general declared utility uu and its density of utility-relevant interactions ρu\rho_{u} (Eq. (14)); the informative interaction density ρinfo\rho_{\mathrm{info}} is the special case in which uu is the expected information gain, and every proof below specializes to it by reading “utility-relevant” as “informative”. We write u⁡(i)=u⁡(i,θt)u(i)=u(i;\theta_{t}) for the true utility of interaction ii and u^(i)=u^ϕ(i∣ℋ0:t)\hat{u}(i)=\hat{u}_{\phi}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}) for its prediction, suppressing arguments not in play. Expectations are over stochastic gradients, predictor outputs, and the interaction stream unless noted. Together, these results make precise what co-design buys and what it risks.

A.1  Proof of Proposition 2

Proposition 2 (restated). Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be finite and κt≤u^tmax\kappa_{t}\leq\hat{u}_{t}^{\max}, so that every maximizer is admissible. As β→∞\beta\to\infty,

πCI(it∣ℋ0:t)⟶[it∈ℐt⋆]|ℐt⋆|,\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}(i_{t}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\;\longrightarrow\;\frac{\mathbf{1}\!\left[i_{t}\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\star}\right]}{|\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\star}|}, (5)

the greedy rule it=arg​maxiu^(i∣ℋ0:t)i_{t}=\argmax_{i}\hat{u}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}) with ties broken uniformly. If the maximizer it⋆i_{t}^{\star} is unique, with gap Δt>0\Delta_{t}>0 to the best other admissible candidate, then

1−πCI(it⋆∣ℋ0:t)≤(|ℐtadm|−1)e−β​Δt,1-\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}(i_{t}^{\star}\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\;\leq\;\bigl(|\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}|-1\bigr)\,e^{-\beta\Delta_{t}}, (6)

so, when |ℐtadm|≥2|\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}|\geq 2, β≥Δt−1​ln⁡((|ℐtadm|−1)/δ)\beta\geq\Delta_{t}^{-1}\ln\bigl((|\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}|-1)/\delta\bigr) selects it⋆i_{t}^{\star} with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta; when |ℐtadm|=1|\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}|=1 it is selected with probability one for every β\beta.

Proof.

Step 1 (Restrict the policy to the admissible set). The indicator in Eq. (3) vanishes outside ℐtadm\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}, so for every i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}

πCI(i∣ℋ0:t)=[i∈ℐtadm]eβ​u^t​(i)∑j∈ℐtadmeβ​u^t​(j).\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})=\frac{\mathbf{1}\!\left[i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}\right]\,e^{\beta\hat{u}_{t}(i)}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}}e^{\beta\hat{u}_{t}(j)}}.

Because κt≤u^tmax\kappa_{t}\leq\hat{u}_{t}^{\max}, every maximizer satisfies u^t​(i)=u^tmax≥κt\hat{u}_{t}(i)=\hat{u}_{t}^{\max}\geq\kappa_{t}, hence ℐt⋆⊆ℐtadm\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\star}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}, the denominator is at least eβ​u^tmax>0e^{\beta\hat{u}_{t}^{\max}}>0, and Zt>0Z_{t}>0.

πCI(i∣ℋ0:t)=[i∈ℐtadm]e−β​dt​(i)∑j∈ℐtadme−β​dt​(j).\pi_{\mathrm{CI}}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})=\frac{\mathbf{1}\!\left[i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}\right]\,e^{-\beta d_{t}(i)}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}}e^{-\beta d_{t}(j)}}.

Step 3 (Limit of the denominator). Split the denominator into maximizers and the rest:

∑j∈ℐtadme−β​dt​(j)=∑j∈ℐt⋆1⏟=|ℐt⋆|+∑j∈ℐtadm∖ℐt⋆e−β​dt​(j).\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}}e^{-\beta d_{t}(j)}=\underbrace{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\star}}1}_{=|\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\star}|}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}\setminus\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\star}}e^{-\beta d_{t}(j)}.

Every term of the second sum has dt​(j)>0d_{t}(j)>0, so it tends to 00 as β→∞\beta\to\infty; the sum is finite because ℐ\mathcal{I} is finite. The denominator therefore converges to |ℐt⋆||\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\star}|.

Step 5 (Rate for a unique maximizer). Let ℐt⋆={it⋆}\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\star}=\{i_{t}^{\star}\} and Sβ=∑j∈ℐtadm∖{it⋆}e−β​dt​(j)S_{\beta}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}\setminus\{i_{t}^{\star}\}}e^{-\beta d_{t}(j)}. which is Eq. (6).

(If |ℐtadm|=1|\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}}|=1 the policy is already deterministic for every β\beta.) ∎

A.2  Proof of Proposition 7

Proposition 7 (restated). Assume dead candidates carry no utility (𝕀¯dead=0\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}}=0, as when umin→0+u_{\min}\to 0^{+} for a non-negative utility), and use the system-level ledger of Eq. (9), in its population form Eq. (11), which charges a predictor cost cpredc_{\text{pred}} to every screened candidate.

  1. 1.

    (Perfect, free predictor.) If exactly the utility-relevant candidates are executed and cpred=0c_{\text{pred}}=0,

    IIECIIIEunc=𝕀¯rel/𝒞¯rel𝕀¯/𝒞¯=1ρu⋅𝒞¯𝒞¯rel= 1+1−ρuρu⋅𝒞¯dead𝒞¯rel,\frac{\mathrm{IIE}^{\mathrm{CI}}}{\mathrm{IIE}^{\text{unc}}}\;=\;\frac{\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}{\bar{\mathbb{I}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}}\;=\;\frac{1}{\rho_{u}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}\;=\;1+\frac{1-\rho_{u}}{\rho_{u}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}, (12)

    which equals 1/ρu1/\rho_{u} when 𝒞¯dead=𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}=\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}} and exceeds it if and only if 𝒞¯dead>𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}>\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}.

  2. 2.

    (Imperfect, costly predictor.) With class-conditional false-positive rate fp\mathrm{fp} (the fraction of dead candidates admitted) and false-negative rate fn\mathrm{fn} (the fraction of utility-relevant candidates suppressed),

    IIECIIIEunc=𝕀¯rel/𝒞¯rel𝕀¯/𝒞¯⋅(1+fp⁡(1−ρu)​𝒞¯dead+cpred(1−fn)​ρu​𝒞¯rel)−1,\frac{\mathrm{IIE}^{\mathrm{CI}}}{\mathrm{IIE}^{\text{unc}}}\;=\;\frac{\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}{\bar{\mathbb{I}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}}\cdot\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{fp}\,(1-\rho_{u})\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}+c_{\text{pred}}}{(1-\mathrm{fn})\,\rho_{u}\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}\right)^{-1}, (13)

    which is non-increasing in each of fp\mathrm{fp}, fn\mathrm{fn} and cpredc_{\text{pred}}, strictly decreasing in any of them whose coefficient is positive, and recovers Eq. (12) as fp,cpred→0\mathrm{fp},c_{\text{pred}}\to 0.

Proof.

Step 1 (Per-candidate accounting). We work with the population efficiency of Eq. (11), the ratio of the expected utility per screened candidate to the expected cost per screened candidate; the finite-stream IIET\mathrm{IIE}_{T} converges to it almost surely for an i.i.d. stream, and for a fixed pool the identities below hold exactly with empirical fractions and class means. We normalize everything per candidate. Recall 𝕀¯=ρu​𝕀¯rel+(1−ρu)​𝕀¯dead\bar{\mathbb{I}}=\rho_{u}\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}+(1-\rho_{u})\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}} and 𝒞¯=ρu​𝒞¯rel+(1−ρu)​𝒞¯dead\bar{\mathcal{C}}=\rho_{u}\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}+(1-\rho_{u})\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}, and the clean case sets 𝕀¯dead=0\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}}=0.

Step 2 (Unconditional interaction). Unconditional interaction executes every candidate, so its utility and cost per candidate are 𝕀¯\bar{\mathbb{I}} and 𝒞¯\bar{\mathcal{C}}, and IIEunc=𝕀¯/𝒞¯\mathrm{IIE}^{\text{unc}}=\bar{\mathbb{I}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}.

Step 3 (Utility under the gate). The gate executes a fraction 1−fn1-\mathrm{fn} of the utility-relevant candidates (mass (1−fn)​ρu(1-\mathrm{fn})\rho_{u}) and a fraction fp\mathrm{fp} of the dead ones (mass fp⁡(1−ρu)\mathrm{fp}(1-\rho_{u})). In the clean case the latter add no utility, so the utility per candidate is

𝕊CI=(1−fn)​ρu​𝕀¯rel.\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{CI}}=(1-\mathrm{fn})\,\rho_{u}\,\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}.

Step 4 (Cost under the gate). Executed utility-relevant candidates cost 𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}} each, executed dead candidates 𝒞¯dead\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}} each, and every candidate is scored at cpredc_{\text{pred}}, so

ℂCI=(1−fn)​ρu​𝒞¯rel+fp⁡(1−ρu)​𝒞¯dead+cpred.\mathbb{C}_{\mathrm{CI}}=(1-\mathrm{fn})\,\rho_{u}\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}+\mathrm{fp}\,(1-\rho_{u})\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}+c_{\text{pred}}.

Step 5 (Factor out the utility-relevant cost). Dividing 𝕊CI\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{CI}} and ℂCI\mathbb{C}_{\mathrm{CI}} by (1−fn)​ρu​𝒞¯rel(1-\mathrm{fn})\rho_{u}\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}} (assume fn<1\mathrm{fn}<1),

IIECI=𝕊CIℂCI=𝕀¯rel𝒞¯rel​(1+g)−1,g=fp⁡(1−ρu)​𝒞¯dead+cpred(1−fn)​ρu​𝒞¯rel.\mathrm{IIE}^{\mathrm{CI}}=\frac{\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{CI}}}{\mathbb{C}_{\mathrm{CI}}}=\frac{\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}\bigl(1+g\bigr)^{-1},\qquad g=\frac{\mathrm{fp}\,(1-\rho_{u})\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}+c_{\text{pred}}}{(1-\mathrm{fn})\,\rho_{u}\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}.

Dividing by IIEunc\mathrm{IIE}^{\text{unc}} from Step 2 gives Eq. (13).

Step 6 (Monotonicity). Write the ratio as K​(1+g)−1K(1+g)^{-1} with K=(𝕀¯rel/𝒞¯rel)/(𝕀¯/𝒞¯)K=(\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}})/(\bar{\mathbb{I}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}) independent of the error rates. The map g↦(1+g)−1g\mapsto(1+g)^{-1} is decreasing, and gg is non-decreasing in fp\mathrm{fp} (coefficient (1−ρu)​𝒞¯dead≥0(1-\rho_{u})\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}\geq 0), in cpredc_{\text{pred}} (coefficient positive), and in fn\mathrm{fn} (through (1−fn)−1(1-\mathrm{fn})^{-1}, which increases on [0,1)[0,1)). Hence the ratio is non-increasing in each, and strictly decreasing whenever the corresponding coefficient is positive.

Step 7 (Ideal case). With fp=cpred=0\mathrm{fp}=c_{\text{pred}}=0, g=0g=0 and the ratio equals KK, the first equality of Eq. (12). Substituting 𝕀¯=ρu​𝕀¯rel\bar{\mathbb{I}}=\rho_{u}\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}},

K=𝕀¯rel𝒞¯rel⋅𝒞¯ρu​𝕀¯rel=1ρu⋅𝒞¯𝒞¯rel,K=\frac{\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}{\rho_{u}\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}}=\frac{1}{\rho_{u}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}},

the second equality. Substituting 𝒞¯\bar{\mathcal{C}},

1ρu⋅ρu​𝒞¯rel+(1−ρu)​𝒞¯dead𝒞¯rel=1+1−ρuρu⋅𝒞¯dead𝒞¯rel,\frac{1}{\rho_{u}}\cdot\frac{\rho_{u}\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}+(1-\rho_{u})\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}=1+\frac{1-\rho_{u}}{\rho_{u}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}},

the third equality.

Step 8 (Comparison with 1/ρu1/\rho_{u}). Subtracting, K−1ρu=1−ρuρu​(𝒞¯dead𝒞¯rel−1)K-\frac{1}{\rho_{u}}=\frac{1-\rho_{u}}{\rho_{u}}\bigl(\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}-1\bigr), which for ρu∈(0,1)\rho_{u}\in(0,1) is zero if and only if 𝒞¯dead=𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}=\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}} and positive if and only if 𝒞¯dead>𝒞¯rel\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}>\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}.

Step 9 (Dead candidates with positive utility). If the zero-utility assumption is dropped, 𝕀¯dead≥0\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}}\geq 0, the perfect free predictor still has IIECI=ρu​𝕀¯rel/(ρu​𝒞¯rel)\mathrm{IIE}^{\mathrm{CI}}=\rho_{u}\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}/(\rho_{u}\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}), so the first equality of Eq. (12) holds unchanged. Since ρu​𝕀¯rel=𝕀¯−(1−ρu)​𝕀¯dead\rho_{u}\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}=\bar{\mathbb{I}}-(1-\rho_{u})\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}},

K=𝒞¯𝒞¯rel⋅𝕀¯rel𝕀¯=1ρu⋅𝒞¯𝒞¯rel​(1−(1−ρu)​𝕀¯dead𝕀¯)≤1ρu⋅𝒞¯𝒞¯rel,K=\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}}{\bar{\mathbb{I}}}=\frac{1}{\rho_{u}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}\Bigl(1-\frac{(1-\rho_{u})\,\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}}}{\bar{\mathbb{I}}}\Bigr)\;\leq\;\frac{1}{\rho_{u}}\cdot\frac{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}{\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}},

with equality if and only if 𝕀¯dead=0\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{dead}}=0 (for ρu<1\rho_{u}<1). The closed forms of Eq. (12) are then upper bounds; this is the relevant case when the floor uminu_{\min} of Eq. (14) is strictly positive. ∎

Remarks. False negatives affect the ratio only through gg: the IIE is utility per unit cost, and suppressed utility-relevant candidates are neither paid for nor counted. Their main effect is on yield, 𝕊CI\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{CI}}, which falls by the factor 1−fn1-\mathrm{fn} and determines how large a pool is needed to reach a target. In the notation of Eq. (10), 𝕊CI\mathbb{S}_{\mathrm{CI}} is the expected yield. Setting cpred=0c_{\text{pred}}=0 recovers execution-only efficiency.

A.3  Proof of Proposition 14

Proposition 14 (restated). Let a pool of nn candidates contain a fraction ρu\rho_{u} of utility-relevant ones, with execution cost cexecc_{\text{exec}}, screening cost cscreen=cembed+cscorec_{\text{screen}}=c_{\text{embed}}+c_{\text{score}} (encoding the candidate and scoring it; this is the cpredc_{\text{pred}} of Eq. (9)), and r=cscreen/cexecr=c_{\text{screen}}/c_{\text{exec}}. With a perfect screen, acquiring the utility-relevant subset costs

𝒞CI𝒞react=ρu+r\frac{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{CI}}}{\mathcal{C}_{\text{react}}}\;=\;\rho_{u}\;+\;r (24)

of what exhaustive execute-then-filter evaluation spends (𝒞react=n​cexec\mathcal{C}_{\text{react}}=n\,c_{\text{exec}}, the baseline that must execute every candidate to find all relevant ones), a speedup approaching 1/ρu1/\rho_{u} as r→0r\to 0, provided a candidate’s utility class cannot be known without executing or scoring it.

Proof.

Step 1 (Information model). We assume that a candidate’s utility class (relevant or dead) cannot be learned without either executing it (reactive evaluation) or scoring it with the predictor (conditional interaction), and that screening costs cscreen=cembed+cpredc_{\text{screen}}=c_{\text{embed}}+c_{\text{pred}}: the predictor head costs cscore=Θ⁡(dϕ2)c_{\text{score}}=\Theta(d_{\phi}^{2}) because it acts on a fixed-size embedding, and encoding the candidate costs cembedc_{\text{embed}}, zero when embeddings are precomputed and cached; neither depends on the rollout length LL or the group size GG.

Step 2 (Reactive cost and its lower bound). A reactive scheme has no signal about an unexecuted candidate. If it skipped a candidate, it could not tell whether that candidate is utility-relevant, so it could not guarantee to acquire the full utility-relevant subset. It must therefore execute all nn candidates:

𝒞react=n​cexec=Θ⁡(n​G​L​dmodel2),\mathcal{C}_{\text{react}}=n\,c_{\text{exec}}=\Theta(n\,G\,L\,d_{\text{model}}^{2}),

which matches Eq. (25). Under the information model of Step 1, no execute-then-filter scheme that must guarantee the full utility-relevant subset can spend less; schemes that sample adaptively, use side information or accept losses fall outside this baseline.

Step 3 (Conditional cost). Conditional interaction encodes and scores all nn candidates, at cost n​cscreenn\,c_{\text{screen}}. A perfect screen then executes exactly the ρu​n\rho_{u}n utility-relevant candidates, at cost ρu​n​cexec\rho_{u}n\,c_{\text{exec}}. Hence

𝒞CI=n​cscreen+ρu​n​cexec,\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{CI}}=n\,c_{\text{screen}}+\rho_{u}\,n\,c_{\text{exec}},

which matches Eq. (26) with B=ρu​nB=\rho_{u}n.

Step 4 (Ratio and speedup). Dividing Step 3 by Step 2,

𝒞CI𝒞react=n​cscreen+ρu​n​cexecn​cexec=ρu+cscreencexec=ρu+r.\frac{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{CI}}}{\mathcal{C}_{\text{react}}}=\frac{n\,c_{\text{screen}}+\rho_{u}n\,c_{\text{exec}}}{n\,c_{\text{exec}}}=\rho_{u}+\frac{c_{\text{screen}}}{c_{\text{exec}}}=\rho_{u}+r.

The speedup is the reciprocal 1/(ρu+r)1/(\rho_{u}+r), which increases to 1/ρu1/\rho_{u} as r→0r\to 0. ∎

A.4  Proof of Proposition 15 and Corollary 16

Proposition 15 (restated). To select the top-BB of nn candidates, synchronous reactive evaluation needs peak memory Mreact​(n)M_{\text{react}}(n), whereas predictive scoring streamed in micro-batches of size bb needs MCI​(n)M_{\mathrm{CI}}(n), where

Mreact​(n)\displaystyle M_{\text{react}}(n) =Θ⁡(n​G​L​dmodel),\displaystyle\;=\;\Theta\!\bigl(n\,G\,L\,d_{\text{model}}\bigr), (27)
MCI​(n)\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{CI}}(n) =Θ⁡(B​G​L​dmodel+b​de+B),\displaystyle\;=\;\Theta\!\bigl(B\,G\,L\,d_{\text{model}}\;+\;b\,d_{e}\;+\;B\bigr), (28)

independent of nn; the pool is then limited only by screening time Θ⁡(n​cpred)\Theta(n\,c_{\text{pred}}) and score storage.

Proof.

Step 1 (Assumptions). (i) Synchronous reactive evaluation keeps each candidate’s in-flight state resident until all outcomes can be compared; this state is Θ⁡(G​L​dmodel)\Theta(GLd_{\text{model}}) per candidate (the KV cache of GG length-LL generations, or trajectory and simulator state). (ii) Predictive scoring needs only the embedding e⁡(τ)∈ℝdee(\tau)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}} and returns a scalar. (iii) Scoring has no side effects.

Step 2 (Reactive peak memory). By (i), at the moment outcomes are compared all nn states are resident, so the peak memory is n⋅Θ⁡(G​L​dmodel)n\cdot\Theta(GLd_{\text{model}}), giving Eq. (27).

Step 3 (Reactive pool cap). Requiring n​Θ​(G​L​dmodel)≤Mn\,\Theta(GLd_{\text{model}})\leq M gives n≤nmaxreact=Θ⁡(M/(G​L​dmodel))n\leq n_{\max}^{\text{react}}=\Theta\bigl(M/(GLd_{\text{model}})\bigr).

Step 4 (Predictive peak memory). Process candidates in micro-batches of size bb. By (ii) and (iii), each embedding can be discarded once its scalar score is recorded, so at most bb embeddings are resident at once: Θ⁡(b​de)\Theta(b\,d_{e}). The scores feed a running top-BB structure: Θ⁡(B)\Theta(B). The only large state is that of the BB executed survivors: Θ⁡(B​G​L​dmodel)\Theta(BGLd_{\text{model}}). Summing the three terms gives Eq. (28), and none of them depends on nn.

Step 5 (What still depends on nn). Screening all candidates takes time Θ⁡(n​cpred)\Theta(n\,c_{\text{pred}}), and storing every score takes Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) memory (or Θ⁡(B)\Theta(B) if only the running top-BB is kept). These, not rollout memory, bound the pool. ∎

Remark (streaming reactive evaluation). If assumption (i) is dropped, a reactive filter can also execute candidates in micro-batches and keep only their scores, giving nn-independent peak memory at Θ⁡(n​cexec)\Theta(n\,c_{\text{exec}}) time. The memory advantage is thus genuine for synchronous pipelines (e.g. group-based advantage estimation holding all GG rollouts of a prompt together, or batched simulators), and otherwise reduces to the time advantage of Proposition 14.

Corollary 16 (restated). The best true utility U(1)nU_{(1)}^{n} among nn i.i.d. candidates is non-decreasing in nn: it converges to the essential supremum if utility is bounded, and grows as nξn^{\xi} (in probability, up to a slowly varying factor) if Pr(U>u)=u−1/ξℓ(u)\Pr(U>u)=u^{-1/\xi}\ell(u). Under predictive sampling this gain costs no additional rollout memory (Eq. (28)), provided the predictor ranks the top of the pool correctly.

Proof.

Let U1,U2,…U_{1},U_{2},\dots be i.i.d. candidate utilities and U(1)n=maxi≤n⁡UiU_{(1)}^{n}=\max_{i\leq n}U_{i}.

Step 1 (Monotonicity). Adding a candidate cannot lower the maximum: U(1)n+1=max⁡(U(1)n,Un+1)≥U(1)nU_{(1)}^{n+1}=\max(U_{(1)}^{n},U_{n+1})\geq U_{(1)}^{n} pointwise, so U(1)nU_{(1)}^{n} is non-decreasing in nn, pointwise and hence stochastically.

Step 2 (Bounded utility). Let u+u^{+} be the essential supremum. For any s>0s>0, ps=Pr⁡(U≤u+−s)<1p_{s}=\Pr(U\leq u^{+}-s)<1 by definition of u+u^{+}, and independence gives Pr⁡(U(1)n≤u+−s)=psn→0\Pr(U_{(1)}^{n}\leq u^{+}-s)=p_{s}^{\,n}\to 0. Hence U(1)n→u+U_{(1)}^{n}\to u^{+} in probability, and almost surely because the sequence is monotone.

Step 3 (Heavy upper tail). Suppose Pr(U>u)=u−1/ξℓ(u)\Pr(U>u)=u^{-1/\xi}\ell(u) with ℓ\ell slowly varying, and choose ana_{n} with Pr⁡(U>an)=1/n\Pr(U>a_{n})=1/n; then ana_{n} is regularly varying in nn with index ξ\xi. For x>0x>0,

Pr(U(1)n≤xan)=(1−Pr(U>xan))n=(1−x−1/ξℓ(xan)n​ℓ​(an))n⟶exp(−x−1/ξ),\Pr\bigl(U_{(1)}^{n}\leq x\,a_{n}\bigr)=\bigl(1-\Pr(U>x\,a_{n})\bigr)^{n}=\Bigl(1-\tfrac{x^{-1/\xi}\ell(xa_{n})}{n\,\ell(a_{n})}\Bigr)^{n}\longrightarrow\exp\bigl(-x^{-1/\xi}\bigr),

using ℓ⁡(x​an)/ℓ⁡(an)→1\ell(xa_{n})/\ell(a_{n})\to 1. This is the Fréchet law, so U(1)n/anU_{(1)}^{n}/a_{n} converges in distribution and U(1)nU_{(1)}^{n} grows as nξn^{\xi} up to a slowly varying factor, in probability. For ξ>1\xi>1 the mean of UU is infinite (for ξ=1\xi=1 it may be, depending on ℓ\ell), so the growth statement is made in probability, not in expectation.

Step 4 (Cost of realizing the growth). By Proposition 15, enlarging the pool leaves peak rollout memory at Eq. (28); by Proposition 14, each extra candidate adds only cpredc_{\text{pred}}. The growth of Steps 2 and 3 concerns the best true utility in the pool; it is realized by the selection only if the predictor ranks the top of the pool correctly, which is quantified by Theorems 18 and 19. ∎

A.5  Proof of Proposition 20

Proposition 20 (restated). Write the expected free energy of interaction ii as

G⁡(i)=−𝔼qϕ​(o∣i)​[ln⁡p⁡(o∣C)]⏟pragmatic value−𝔼qϕ​(o∣i)[DKL[qϕ(θ∣o,i)∥qϕ(θ∣i)]]⏟epistemic value,G(i)=\underbrace{-\,\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(o\mid i)}\!\bigl[\ln p(o\mid C)\bigr]}_{\text{pragmatic value}}-\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(o\mid i)}\!\bigl[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[q_{\phi}(\theta\mid o,i)\,\Big\|\,q_{\phi}(\theta\mid i)\right]\bigr]}_{\text{epistemic value}}, (35)

with preferences p⁡(o∣C)p(o\mid C) over a finite outcome space 𝒪\mathcal{O}. If preferences are uniform and cost is accounted separately through 𝒞⁡(i)\mathcal{C}(i), then

arg​mini∈ℐ⁡G​(i)=arg​maxi∈ℐ⁡Iqϕ​(θ;o∣i)=arg​maxi∈ℐ⁡𝒰IGqϕ​(i∣ℋt),\argmin_{i\in\mathcal{I}}G(i)=\argmax_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\;I_{q_{\phi}}(\theta;o\mid i)=\argmax_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\;\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}^{q_{\phi}}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}), (36)

where 𝒰IGqϕ\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}^{q_{\phi}} is Eq. (32) evaluated under the variational model qϕq_{\phi}, and coincides with 𝒰IG\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}} when qϕq_{\phi} is the exact posterior and predictive. Under non-uniform preferences the two criteria diverge.

Proof.

Step 1 (Well-posedness). Assume qϕ​(θ∣o,i)q_{\phi}(\theta\mid o,i) is absolutely continuous with respect to qϕ​(θ∣i)q_{\phi}(\theta\mid i) for every oo and ii, so all divergences below are finite.

Step 2 (The pragmatic term is constant). Under uniform preferences p⁡(o∣C)=1/|𝒪|p(o\mid C)=1/|\mathcal{O}|, so −ln⁡p⁡(o∣C)=ln⁡|𝒪|-\ln p(o\mid C)=\ln|\mathcal{O}| for every oo, and its expectation under any qϕ​(o∣i)q_{\phi}(o\mid i) is ln⁡|𝒪|\ln|\mathcal{O}|, independent of ii.

Step 3 (Reduce to the epistemic term). Subtracting a constant does not change a minimizer, and minimizing the negative of a quantity is maximizing it, so by Eq. (35)

arg​mini⁡G​(i)\displaystyle\argmin_{i}G(i) =arg​mini(−𝔼qϕ​(o∣i)[DKL[qϕ(θ∣o,i)∥qϕ(θ∣i)]])\displaystyle=\argmin_{i}\Bigl(-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(o\mid i)}\bigl[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[q_{\phi}(\theta\mid o,i)\,\Big\|\,q_{\phi}(\theta\mid i)\right]\bigr]\Bigr) (58)
=arg​maxi𝔼qϕ​(o∣i)[DKL[qϕ(θ∣o,i)∥qϕ(θ∣i)]].\displaystyle=\argmax_{i}\;\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(o\mid i)}\bigl[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[q_{\phi}(\theta\mid o,i)\,\Big\|\,q_{\phi}(\theta\mid i)\right]\bigr].

Step 4 (The epistemic term is a mutual information). Write the divergence as an expectation and use Bayes’ rule, qϕ​(θ∣o,i)/qϕ​(θ∣i)=qϕ​(θ,o∣i)/[qϕ​(θ∣i)​qϕ​(o∣i)]q_{\phi}(\theta\mid o,i)/q_{\phi}(\theta\mid i)=q_{\phi}(\theta,o\mid i)/[q_{\phi}(\theta\mid i)\,q_{\phi}(o\mid i)]:

𝔼qϕ​(o∣i)​[𝔼qϕ​(θ∣o,i)​ln⁡qϕ​(θ∣o,i)qϕ​(θ∣i)]=𝔼qϕ​(θ,o∣i)​[ln⁡qϕ​(θ,o∣i)qϕ​(θ∣i)​qϕ​(o∣i)]=Iqϕ​(θ;o∣i).\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(o\mid i)}\!\Bigl[\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\theta\mid o,i)}\ln\frac{q_{\phi}(\theta\mid o,i)}{q_{\phi}(\theta\mid i)}\Bigr]=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\theta,o\mid i)}\!\left[\ln\frac{q_{\phi}(\theta,o\mid i)}{q_{\phi}(\theta\mid i)\,q_{\phi}(o\mid i)}\right]=I_{q_{\phi}}(\theta;o\mid i). (59)

Step 5 (Identify the utility). By definition, 𝒰IGqϕ​(i∣ℋt)\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}^{q_{\phi}}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}) is the expected posterior-to-prior divergence of Eq. (32) with pp replaced by qϕq_{\phi}, which by Eq. (59) equals Iqϕ​(θ;o∣i)I_{q_{\phi}}(\theta;o\mid i). Combining Steps 3 and 4 gives Eq. (36). If qϕq_{\phi} is the exact posterior and predictive, 𝒰IGqϕ=𝒰IG\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}^{q_{\phi}}=\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{IG}}; otherwise the maximizer is that of the variational surrogate, not necessarily of the true information gain.

Step 6 (Non-uniform preferences). If p⁡(o∣C)p(o\mid C) is not uniform, the pragmatic term depends on ii through qϕ​(o∣i)q_{\phi}(o\mid i), it no longer drops out in Step 3, and the minimizer of GG trades information gain against preference satisfaction. ∎

A.6  Proof of Theorem 18 and Corollary 19

Theorem 18 (restated). Assume (i) selection is the deterministic limit of the fixed-size batch rule Eq. (47) with μ=0\mu=0 and 𝒜\mathcal{A} the predicted utility u^\hat{u}, the cardinality-constrained form of the master objective Eq. (15), so each round retains the top-BB set by u^\hat{u}; (ii) εϕ=sup0≤t<Tsupi∈ℐt|u^t​(i)−ut​(i)|\varepsilon_{\phi}=\sup_{0\leq t<T}\sup_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}\left|\hat{u}_{t}(i)-u_{t}(i)\right|, a time-uniform error, with u^t(i)=u^ϕt(i∣ℋ0:t)\hat{u}_{t}(i)=\hat{u}_{\phi_{t}}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t}); and (iii) gapmin=mint⁡mini∈ℬt∗,j∈ℐt∖ℬt∗⁡(ut​(i)−ut​(j))>0\mathrm{gap}_{\min}=\min_{t}\min_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*},\,j\in\mathcal{I}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}}\bigl(u_{t}(i)-u_{t}(j)\bigr)>0. Then

ℛT(πCI,π∗)≤ 2TBεϕ⋅[2εϕ≥gapmin];\mathcal{R}_{T}(\pi_{\mathrm{CI}},\pi^{*})\;\leq\;2\,T\,B\,\varepsilon_{\phi}\,\cdot\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[2\varepsilon_{\phi}\geq\mathrm{gap}_{\min}\right]; (30)

in particular, the selection is exactly the oracle’s whenever 2​εϕ<gapmin2\varepsilon_{\phi}<\mathrm{gap}_{\min}. More generally, with round-specific errors εt=supi∈ℐt|u^t​(i)−ut​(i)|\varepsilon_{t}=\sup_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}\left|\hat{u}_{t}(i)-u_{t}(i)\right| and gaps gapt\mathrm{gap}_{t}, ℛT≤∑t<T2Bεt[2εt≥gapt]\mathcal{R}_{T}\leq\sum_{t<T}2B\varepsilon_{t}\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[2\varepsilon_{t}\geq\mathrm{gap}_{t}\right].

Proof.

Step 1 (Per-round regret). By Eq. (29), ℛT=∑t=0T−1rt\mathcal{R}_{T}=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}r_{t} with rt=∑i∈ℬt∗ut​(i)−∑i∈ℬ^tut​(i)r_{t}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}}u_{t}(i)-\sum_{i\in\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{t}}u_{t}(i). It suffices to bound each rtr_{t}. Fix a round tt and, in Steps 2–6, write u=utu=u_{t} and u^=u^t\hat{u}=\hat{u}_{t}; by the time-uniform assumption (ii), |u^​(i)−u⁡(i)|≤εϕ\left|\hat{u}(i)-u(i)\right|\leq\varepsilon_{\phi} for every i∈ℐti\in\mathcal{I}_{t}.

Step 2 (Only swapped items contribute). Write ℬt∗∖ℬ^t={i1,…,im}\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}\setminus\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{t}=\{i_{1},\dots,i_{m}\} (oracle items missed) and ℬ^t∖ℬt∗={j1,…,jm}\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}=\{j_{1},\dots,j_{m}\} (wrong items selected). Both sets have the same size m≤Bm\leq B because both selections have size BB. Items in ℬt∗∩ℬ^t\mathcal{B}_{t}^{*}\cap\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{t} cancel, so

rt=∑k=1m[u⁡(ik)−u⁡(jk)]r_{t}=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\bigl[u(i_{k})-u(j_{k})\bigr] (60)

for any pairing of the two sets.

Step 4 (Each swap costs at most 2​εϕ2\varepsilon_{\phi}). By (ii), u⁡(ik)≤u^​(ik)+εϕu(i_{k})\leq\hat{u}(i_{k})+\varepsilon_{\phi} and u⁡(jk)≥u^​(jk)−εϕu(j_{k})\geq\hat{u}(j_{k})-\varepsilon_{\phi}. Subtracting and using Step 3,

u⁡(ik)−u⁡(jk)≤u^​(ik)−u^​(jk)+2​εϕ≤2​εϕ.u(i_{k})-u(j_{k})\leq\hat{u}(i_{k})-\hat{u}(j_{k})+2\varepsilon_{\phi}\leq 2\varepsilon_{\phi}. (61)
