Both sides are in the units of the declared utility (nats when uu is information gain); gapmin\mathrm{gap}_{\min} enters only through the indicator. ∎

Corollary 19 (restated). Suppose each round’s pool has at most nn candidates; for every round tt and every candidate outside a blind-spot set 𝒪t⊆ℐt\mathcal{O}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{t} with |𝒪t|≤nood|\mathcal{O}_{t}|\leq n_{\mathrm{ood}}, the error u^t​(i)−ut​(i)\hat{u}_{t}(i)-u_{t}(i) is zero-mean and σϕ\sigma_{\phi}-sub-Gaussian, while errors on 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} are unrestricted; and the utility takes values in an interval of length umaxu_{\max} (e.g. u∈[0,umax]u\in[0,u_{\max}]). Then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta and εϕeff=σϕ​2​ln⁡(2​n​T/δ)\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}=\sigma_{\phi}\sqrt{2\ln(2nT/\delta)},

ℛT(πCI,π∗)≤ 2TBεϕeff[2εϕeff≥gapmin]+Tmin(B,nood)umax.\mathcal{R}_{T}(\pi_{\mathrm{CI}},\pi^{*})\;\leq\;2\,T\,B\,\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[2\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}\geq\mathrm{gap}_{\min}\right]\;+\;T\,\min(B,n_{\mathrm{ood}})\,u_{\max}. (31)
Proof.

Step 1 (Tail bound for one candidate). A zero-mean σϕ\sigma_{\phi}-sub-Gaussian error satisfies Pr(|u^t(i)−ut(i)|>s)≤2e−s2/(2σϕ2)\Pr\bigl(|\hat{u}_{t}(i)-u_{t}(i)|>s\bigr)\leq 2e^{-s^{2}/(2\sigma_{\phi}^{2})} for all s>0s>0.

Step 2 (Union bound over candidates and rounds). There are at most n​TnT candidate–round pairs outside the blind spots 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t}. Setting s=εϕeff=σϕ​2​ln⁡(2​n​T/δ)s=\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}=\sigma_{\phi}\sqrt{2\ln(2nT/\delta)} makes each tail probability at most δ/(n​T)\delta/(nT), so with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta every error outside the blind spots in every round is at most εϕeff\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}. The rest of the proof works on this event.

Step 3 (Classify swapped pairs). In round tt, pair the swapped items as in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 18. Call a pair clean if neither of its items lies in 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} and contaminated otherwise.

Step 4 (Clean pairs). Steps 3–5 of the proof of Theorem 18 apply verbatim with εϕeff\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}} in place of εϕ\varepsilon_{\phi}: each clean pair costs at most 2​εϕeff2\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}} and exists only if 2​εϕeff≥gapmin2\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}\geq\mathrm{gap}_{\min}. There are at most BB of them, contributing at most 2Bεϕeff[2εϕeff≥gapmin]2B\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[2\varepsilon_{\phi}^{\mathrm{eff}}\geq\mathrm{gap}_{\min}\right].

Step 5 (Contaminated pairs). Each item appears in at most one pair, so at most noodn_{\mathrm{ood}} pairs contain a blind-spot item, and at most BB pairs exist in total; hence there are at most min⁡(B,nood)\min(B,n_{\mathrm{ood}}) contaminated pairs. Since the utility ranges over an interval of length umaxu_{\max}, each costs u⁡(ik)−u⁡(jk)≤umaxu(i_{k})-u(j_{k})\leq u_{\max}.

Step 6 (Sum over rounds). Adding Steps 4 and 5 and summing over TT rounds gives Eq. (31) on the event of Step 2. ∎

Remark. The blind-spot term is stated as a count rather than a pool fraction deliberately: selection by u^\hat{u} preferentially admits candidates whose utility is overestimated, so a single blind spot with unbounded overestimation is selected with certainty, and a bound of the form B​δood​umaxB\,\delta_{\mathrm{ood}}u_{\max}, with δood\delta_{\mathrm{ood}} the blind-spot fraction, would not hold in general. If utilities are tied at the BB-th position (gapmin=0\mathrm{gap}_{\min}=0), the indicators are always active and the bounds degrade linearly in the error.

A.7  Proof of Lemma 21

Lemma 21 (restated). Let candidates i∼𝒟i\sim\mathcal{D} be utility-relevant when u⁡(i)≥uminu(i)\geq u_{\min}, let the gate admit ii when u^​(i)≥umin\hat{u}(i)\geq u_{\min}, and suppose |u^​(i)−u⁡(i)|≤ε\left|\hat{u}(i)-u(i)\right|\leq\varepsilon for every ii. More generally, let the gate admit ii when u^​(i)≥κ\hat{u}(i)\geq\kappa. Every misclassified candidate, admitted while dead or suppressed while relevant, then lies in the band ℬε={i:κ−ε≤u⁡(i)<umin}∪{i:umin≤u⁡(i)<κ+ε}\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}=\{i:\kappa-\varepsilon\leq u(i)<u_{\min}\}\cup\{i:u_{\min}\leq u(i)<\kappa+\varepsilon\}, so the misclassified masses satisfy δFP+δFN≤Pri∼𝒟⁡(ℬε)\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}+\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}\leq\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}). With κ=umin\kappa=u_{\min}, if the true utility satisfies the margin condition Pri∼𝒟⁡(|u⁡(i)−umin|≤ε)≤m​ε\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}}\bigl(\left|u(i)-u_{\min}\right|\leq\varepsilon\bigr)\leq m\,\varepsilon with constant mm, then the gate misclassifies, by admitting a dead candidate or suppressing a relevant one, at most a fraction m​εm\,\varepsilon of candidates.

Proof.

Let the gate admit ii when u^​(i)≥κ\hat{u}(i)\geq\kappa; the lemma’s first statement is the case κ=umin\kappa=u_{\min}.

Step 1 (A false negative lies in the upper part of the band). A relevant candidate is suppressed when u⁡(i)≥uminu(i)\geq u_{\min} and u^​(i)<κ\hat{u}(i)<\kappa. Then u⁡(i)≤u^​(i)+ε<κ+εu(i)\leq\hat{u}(i)+\varepsilon<\kappa+\varepsilon, so u(i)∈[umin,κ+ε)u(i)\in[u_{\min},\kappa+\varepsilon).

Step 2 (A false positive lies in the lower part of the band). A dead candidate is admitted when u⁡(i)<uminu(i)<u_{\min} and u^​(i)≥κ\hat{u}(i)\geq\kappa. Then u⁡(i)≥u^​(i)−ε≥κ−εu(i)\geq\hat{u}(i)-\varepsilon\geq\kappa-\varepsilon, so u(i)∈[κ−ε,umin)u(i)\in[\kappa-\varepsilon,u_{\min}).

Step 3 (Count). Every misclassified candidate therefore lies in ℬε\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}, so δFP+δFN≤Pri∼𝒟⁡(ℬε)\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}+\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}\leq\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}}(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}). With κ=umin\kappa=u_{\min}, ℬε⊆{i:|u⁡(i)−umin|≤ε}\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon}\subseteq\{i:\left|u(i)-u_{\min}\right|\leq\varepsilon\}, whose probability under 𝒟\mathcal{D} is at most m​εm\varepsilon by the margin condition. ∎

A.8  Proof of Proposition 22 and Proposition 23

Proposition 22 (restated). Let 𝒜tt\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tt}} be the queries on which the full budget is more accurate in expectation than one increment, with density ρacctt\rho_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\mathrm{tt}}, and let the gate threshold a declared test-time utility whose relevant set contains 𝒜tt\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tt}}, with density ρutt≥ρacctt\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}}\geq\rho_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\mathrm{tt}}. Let unconditional scaling spend CC unit increments per query, let the answer be a function of the belief state, and let the selection policy be the one-probe gate: it spends one probing increment plus cpredc_{\text{pred}} and then halts or continues to the full budget, with δFN\delta_{\mathrm{FN}} and δFP\delta_{\mathrm{FP}} the fractions of all queries that are relevant but halted and dead but continued. Then the gated policy loses at most δFN\delta_{\mathrm{FN}} accuracy while spending at most a fraction

ρutt+1+cpredC+δFP\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}}+\frac{1+c_{\text{pred}}}{C}+\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}

of the unconditional compute, a multiplier approaching 1/ρutt1/\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}} as C→∞C\to\infty and δFP→0\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}\to 0. By Lemma 21, δFN+δFP≤Pr⁡(ℬεϕ)\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}+\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}\leq\Pr(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon_{\phi}}) for a predictor with error at most εϕ\varepsilon_{\phi}, which is at most m​εϕm\varepsilon_{\phi} under the margin condition. The tightest choice is the accuracy-gain utility itself, for which ρutt=ρacctt\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}}=\rho_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\mathrm{tt}}. The continuation utility of Eq. (51) with umin→0+u_{\min}\to 0^{+} is also admissible: if its value is zero then bC=b1b_{C}=b_{1} almost surely, so the answer, and with it the accuracy, is unchanged; its gate should use κ>εϕ\kappa>\varepsilon_{\phi}, so that the atom of zero-utility queries is never admitted. With density ρconttt≥ρacctt\rho_{\mathrm{cont}}^{\mathrm{tt}}\geq\rho_{\mathrm{acc}}^{\mathrm{tt}} it gives the weaker multiplier 1/ρconttt1/\rho_{\mathrm{cont}}^{\mathrm{tt}}. The next-step utility of Eq. (49) is admissible only under the no-delayed-gain condition.

Proof.

Step 1 (Assumptions made explicit). (i) Unconditional scaling spends CC unit-cost increments on every query. (ii) Every query outside the relevant set RR of the declared utility lies outside 𝒜tt\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tt}}, so its expected accuracy after the first increment is at least that after CC increments. For the continuation utility of Eq. (51) with umin→0+u_{\min}\to 0^{+} this holds because a query outside RR has 𝔼[DKL[bC∥b1]]=0\mathbb{E}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[b_{C}\,\Big\|\,b_{1}\right]]=0; the divergence is non-negative, so bC=b1b_{C}=b_{1} almost surely, and since the answer is a function of the belief state, the answer and its expected accuracy are unchanged. For the next-step utility of Eq. (49) the same conclusion needs the no-delayed-gain condition, because a zero next-step change does not rule out later changes. (iii) The gated policy spends one probing increment, pays cpredc_{\text{pred}} for its prediction, and then either halts or continues to the full budget CC. (iv) Per-query accuracy lies in [0,1][0,1].

Step 2 (Partition of queries). Let ρ=ρutt\rho=\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{tt}}. Each query falls into one of four classes: relevant and continued (fraction ρ−δFN\rho-\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}), relevant but halted (false negatives, δFN\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}), dead and halted (1−ρ−δFP1-\rho-\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}), and dead but continued (false positives, δFP\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}); these are unconditional masses of the whole query pool, not the class-conditional rates fp,fn\mathrm{fp},\mathrm{fn} of Proposition 7. By Lemma 21, δFN+δFP≤Pr⁡(ℬεϕ)\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}+\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}\leq\Pr(\mathcal{B}_{\varepsilon_{\phi}}), which is at most m​εϕm\varepsilon_{\phi} under the margin condition.

Step 3 (Accuracy class by class). Continued queries, relevant or not, receive the full budget and give exactly the unconditional answer. Correctly halted dead queries are, by (ii), at least as accurate as under the full budget. Only false negatives can lose accuracy, and by (iv) each loses at most one unit. Hence the accuracy loss is at most δFN\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}.

Step 4 (Compute). Every query costs cpredc_{\text{pred}} for prediction, plus CC if continued or 11 if halted. The continued fraction is ρ−δFN+δFP≤ρ+δFP\rho-\delta_{\mathrm{FN}}+\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}\leq\rho+\delta_{\mathrm{FP}} and the halted fraction is at most 11, so the expected cost per query is at most

(ρ+δFP)​C+1+cpred.(\rho+\delta_{\mathrm{FP}})\,C+1+c_{\text{pred}}.

Step 5 (Compute fraction). Dividing by the unconditional cost CC gives the upper bound ρ+1+cpredC+δFP\rho+\frac{1+c_{\text{pred}}}{C}+\delta_{\mathrm{FP}} on the compute fraction stated in the proposition, which tends to ρ\rho as C→∞C\to\infty and δFP→0\delta_{\mathrm{FP}}\to 0; the multiplier then approaches 1/ρ1/\rho. ∎

Proposition 23 (restated). Suppose (a) omitting any set of decision-irrelevant actions leaves the answer unchanged; (b) the gate thresholds a predicted relevance score with error at most εϕ\varepsilon_{\phi}, and on every task the action scores satisfy the margin condition of Lemma 21 with constant mm, so that in expectation at most a fraction m​εϕm\,\varepsilon_{\phi} of the actions are misclassified; and (c) prediction costs a fraction rr of an average action. Consider tasks with NN candidate actions in which no action costs more than RcR_{c} times the task’s average action cost. If utility-relevant actions carry a share ρu𝒞\rho_{u}^{\mathcal{C}} of the expected call-everything cost (the cost-weighted density of utility-relevant actions, which reduces to their fraction ρu\rho_{u} when all actions cost the same), the conditional agent’s accuracy is within N​m​εϕNm\,\varepsilon_{\phi} of call-everything accuracy, at expected cost

𝔼⁡[𝒞CI]≤(ρu𝒞+r+m​εϕ​Rc)​𝔼​[𝒞all].\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{CI}}]\;\leq\;\bigl(\rho_{u}^{\mathcal{C}}+r+m\,\varepsilon_{\phi}\,R_{c}\bigr)\,\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{C}_{\text{all}}].
Proof.

Step 1 (Setup). Consider a task with NN candidate actions with costs c1,…,cN≤cmaxc_{1},\dots,c_{N}\leq c_{\max} and total Call=∑kckC_{\text{all}}=\sum_{k}c_{k}, so the average action costs c¯=Call/N\bar{c}=C_{\text{all}}/N and, by assumption, cmax≤Rc​c¯c_{\max}\leq R_{c}\,\bar{c}. The predictor costs r​c¯r\bar{c} per action, r​CallrC_{\text{all}} in total.

Step 2 (Accuracy). Let ℰ\mathcal{E} be the set of actions the conditional agent executes, and ℰrel\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{rel}} the set of utility-relevant actions. If there is no false negative, ℰ⊇ℰrel\mathcal{E}\supseteq\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{rel}}, so ℰ\mathcal{E} differs from the call-everything set only by omitting some decision-irrelevant actions, and by (a) the committed answer is unchanged. The answer can therefore differ only on the event that at least one false negative occurs. Conditional on the task, by (b) and Markov’s inequality, this event has probability at most 𝔼⁡[#​false negatives]≤m​εϕ​N\mathbb{E}[\#\text{false negatives}]\leq m\varepsilon_{\phi}N, which bounds the accuracy loss; averaging over tasks preserves the bound. The loss grows with the task length NN.

Step 3 (Cost of one task). The conditional agent pays the predictor on every action (r​CallrC_{\text{all}}), the full cost on executed relevant actions (at most the task’s relevant cost Crel=∑k∈ℰrelckC_{\text{rel}}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{rel}}}c_{k}), and the full cost on false positives, each at most cmax≤Rc​c¯c_{\max}\leq R_{c}\bar{c}. Conditional on the task, by (b) the expected number of false positives is at most m​εϕ​Nm\varepsilon_{\phi}N, so

𝔼⁡[CCI∣task]≤r​Call+Crel+m​εϕ​N​Rc​c¯=r​Call+Crel+m​εϕ​Rc​Call.\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{CI}}\mid\text{task}]\leq rC_{\text{all}}+C_{\text{rel}}+m\varepsilon_{\phi}NR_{c}\bar{c}=rC_{\text{all}}+C_{\text{rel}}+m\varepsilon_{\phi}R_{c}\,C_{\text{all}}.

Step 4 (Take expectations over tasks). By definition of the cost-weighted density, 𝔼⁡[Crel]=ρu𝒞​𝔼​[Call]\mathbb{E}[C_{\text{rel}}]=\rho_{u}^{\mathcal{C}}\,\mathbb{E}[C_{\text{all}}]. Averaging Step 3 over tasks therefore gives

𝔼⁡[CCI]≤(ρu𝒞+r+m​εϕ​Rc)​𝔼​[Call],\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{CI}}]\leq\bigl(\rho_{u}^{\mathcal{C}}+r+m\varepsilon_{\phi}R_{c}\bigr)\,\mathbb{E}[C_{\text{all}}],

the stated bound with every constant explicit. When all actions cost the same, Crel/CallC_{\text{rel}}/C_{\text{all}} is the fraction of relevant actions and ρu𝒞\rho_{u}^{\mathcal{C}} reduces to ρu\rho_{u}. ∎

Remark. Separability is essential. If two individually irrelevant actions are jointly relevant (for instance, two retrievals whose combination answers the question), suppressing both can change the answer, and the accuracy statement fails.

A.9  Proof of Proposition 12

Proposition 12 (restated). Assume equal costs, a budget of BB executions, and that each candidate’s utility depends on the predictor outputs only through its own, 𝔼⁡[U⁡(i)∣U^]=𝔼⁡[U⁡(i)∣U^​(i)]\mathbb{E}[U(i)\mid\hat{U}]=\mathbb{E}[U(i)\mid\hat{U}(i)]. Then, among all selection rules that see only the predictor outputs U^\hat{U}, executing the BB candidates with the largest posterior mean 𝔼⁡[U∣U^]\mathbb{E}[U\mid\hat{U}] maximizes expected executed utility and hence the IIE. Setting κt\kappa_{t} to the BB-th largest posterior mean makes the admissible set of Eq. (3) exactly that top-BB set, up to ties at the BB-th value.

Proof.

Step 1 (Admissible rules). A selection rule that depends on the candidates only through their predictor outputs chooses a set SS of size BB that is a function of U^=(U^​(1),…,U^​(n))\hat{U}=(\hat{U}(1),\dots,\hat{U}(n)) (and possibly of independent randomization).

Step 2 (IIE reduces to executed utility). With equal costs 𝒞¯\bar{\mathcal{C}}, a constant scoring cost cpredc_{\text{pred}} for each of the nn screened candidates, and exactly BB executions, the IIE denominator in Eq. (9) equals n​cpred+B​𝒞¯n\,c_{\text{pred}}+B\bar{\mathcal{C}} for every such SS, so maximizing IIE is equivalent to maximizing 𝔼⁡[∑i∈SU⁡(i)]\mathbb{E}\bigl[\sum_{i\in S}U(i)\bigr].

Step 3 (Tower property). Because SS is determined by U^\hat{U},

𝔼⁡[∑i∈SU⁡(i)]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[∑i∈SU⁡(i)|U^]]=𝔼⁡[∑i∈S𝔼⁡[U⁡(i)∣U^]].\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{i\in S}U(i)\Bigr]=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\,\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{i\in S}U(i)\,\Big|\,\hat{U}\Bigr]\Bigr]=\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{i\in S}\mathbb{E}\bigl[U(i)\mid\hat{U}\bigr]\Bigr].

Step 4 (Locality). Assume that each candidate’s utility depends on the predictor outputs only through its own output, i.e. 𝔼⁡[U⁡(i)∣U^]=𝔼⁡[U⁡(i)∣U^​(i)]=:μ⁡(U^​(i))\mathbb{E}[U(i)\mid\hat{U}]=\mathbb{E}[U(i)\mid\hat{U}(i)]=:\mu(\hat{U}(i)).

Step 5 (Pointwise optimization). For each realization of U^\hat{U}, the inner sum ∑i∈Sμ​(U^​(i))\sum_{i\in S}\mu(\hat{U}(i)) over sets of size BB is maximized by the BB largest values of μ​(U^​(i))\mu(\hat{U}(i)): exchanging any selected item for an unselected one with a larger value increases the sum. The top-BB rule is therefore optimal for every realization, hence in expectation, and randomization cannot help.

Step 6 (Realization by the gate). Setting u^=μ⁡(U^)=𝔼⁡[U∣U^]\hat{u}=\mu(\hat{U})=\mathbb{E}[U\mid\hat{U}] and κt\kappa_{t} to the BB-th largest of these values makes the admissible set ℐtadm\mathcal{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{adm}} of Eq. (4) exactly the top-BB set of Step 5 (when several candidates tie at the BB-th value, the admissible set contains all of them and ties are broken arbitrarily, which leaves the executed utility unchanged), so executing the admissible set realizes the optimum. This is the thresholding half of Eq. (3); the sampling half is irrelevant here, since the whole admissible set is executed, and the batch rule is the cardinality-constrained form of Eq. (47) rather than the single-draw limit of Proposition 2. ∎

Remark (relation to the information bottleneck). Stationary points of Eq. (21) satisfy the self-consistent IB equations (Tishby et al., 2000), q(U^∣ℋ)∝q(U^)exp(−βIBDKL[p(U∣ℋ)∥p(U∣U^)])q(\hat{U}\mid\mathcal{H})\propto q(\hat{U})\exp\bigl(-\beta_{\mathrm{IB}}\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[p(U\mid\mathcal{H})\,\Big\|\,p(U\mid\hat{U})\right]\bigr). Stationarity does not imply that U^\hat{U} is the most informative feature of its complexity, and a higher I⁡(U^,U)I(\hat{U};U) does not by itself guarantee better top-BB selection. The proposition therefore makes no claim about which U^\hat{U} is optimal, only about how to use a given one.

A.10  Proof of Proposition 13

Proposition 13 (restated). Assume the setting of Proposition 7(ii); that ρu\rho_{u}, fp⁡(s)\mathrm{fp}(s) and fn⁡(s)<1\mathrm{fn}(s)<1 do not depend on kk; that cpred​(s)/(1−fn⁡(s))c_{\text{pred}}(s)/(1-\mathrm{fn}(s)) is non-decreasing in ss; and that the IIE ratio Eq. (13) attains its maximum over 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} for every kk, on a set S⋆​(k)S^{\star}(k) of optimal System-1 sizes. Then (i) S⋆S^{\star} is non-decreasing in kk in the strong set order: if k′>kk^{\prime}>k, s∈S⋆​(k)s\in S^{\star}(k) and s′∈S⋆​(k′)s^{\prime}\in S^{\star}(k^{\prime}), then max⁡(s,s′)∈S⋆​(k′)\max(s,s^{\prime})\in S^{\star}(k^{\prime}) and min⁡(s,s′)∈S⋆​(k)\min(s,s^{\prime})\in S^{\star}(k), so the largest and the smallest optimal sizes, where they exist, are non-decreasing in kk; and (ii) the maximal IIE ratio is non-decreasing in kk.

Proof.

Step 1 (The ratio in terms of ss and kk). Write 𝒞¯rel,𝒞¯dead\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}},\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}} for the execution costs at k=1k=1. After scaling System 2 they become k​𝒞¯relk\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}} and k​𝒞¯deadk\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}, so the pool mean 𝒞¯\bar{\mathcal{C}} also scales by kk. The first factor of Eq. (13), (𝕀¯rel/𝒞¯rel)/(𝕀¯/𝒞¯)=𝕀¯rel​𝒞¯/(𝕀¯​𝒞¯rel)(\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}})/(\bar{\mathbb{I}}/\bar{\mathcal{C}})=\bar{\mathbb{I}}_{\text{rel}}\bar{\mathcal{C}}/(\bar{\mathbb{I}}\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}), is a ratio of two costs and is therefore unchanged by kk; it does not depend on ss either, and we call it K>0K>0. Dividing numerator and denominator of the overhead term by kk,

IIECIIIEunc​(s,k)=K1+h⁡(s,k),h⁡(s,k)=a⁡(s)+b⁡(s)k,\frac{\mathrm{IIE}^{\mathrm{CI}}}{\mathrm{IIE}^{\text{unc}}}(s,k)\;=\;\frac{K}{1+h(s,k)},\qquad h(s,k)\;=\;a(s)+\frac{b(s)}{k},

with

a⁡(s)=fp⁡(s)​(1−ρu)​𝒞¯dead(1−fn⁡(s))​ρu​𝒞¯rel,b⁡(s)=cpred​(s)(1−fn⁡(s))​ρu​𝒞¯rel.a(s)=\frac{\mathrm{fp}(s)\,(1-\rho_{u})\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{dead}}}{(1-\mathrm{fn}(s))\,\rho_{u}\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}},\qquad b(s)=\frac{c_{\text{pred}}(s)}{(1-\mathrm{fn}(s))\,\rho_{u}\,\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}}}.

By assumption neither aa nor bb depends on kk, and b≥0b\geq 0.

Step 2 (Reduction to minimizing hh). Since x↦K/(1+x)x\mapsto K/(1+x) is strictly decreasing on x≥0x\geq 0, maximizing the IIE ratio over ss is equivalent to minimizing h⁡(⋅,k)h(\cdot,k), and S⋆​(k)=arg​mins∈𝒮1⁡h​(s,k)S^{\star}(k)=\argmin_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{1}}h(s,k). Put t=1/kt=1/k, so that increasing kk means decreasing tt, and h=a⁡(s)+b⁡(s)​th=a(s)+b(s)\,t.

Step 3 (Increasing differences). The factor ρu​𝒞¯rel\rho_{u}\bar{\mathcal{C}}_{\text{rel}} is a positive constant, so bb is non-decreasing in ss by the assumption on cpred/(1−fn)c_{\text{pred}}/(1-\mathrm{fn}). Hence for s′≥ss^{\prime}\geq s the difference

h⁡(s′,t)−h⁡(s,t)=a⁡(s′)−a⁡(s)+(b⁡(s′)−b⁡(s))​th(s^{\prime},t)-h(s,t)\;=\;a(s^{\prime})-a(s)+\bigl(b(s^{\prime})-b(s)\bigr)\,t

is non-decreasing in tt.

Step 4 (Strong set order). Let k′>kk^{\prime}>k, i.e. t′=1/k′<t=1/kt^{\prime}=1/k^{\prime}<t=1/k, and take s∈S⋆​(k)s\in S^{\star}(k), s′∈S⋆​(k′)s^{\prime}\in S^{\star}(k^{\prime}). If s≤s′s\leq s^{\prime} then max⁡(s,s′)=s′\max(s,s^{\prime})=s^{\prime} and min⁡(s,s′)=s\min(s,s^{\prime})=s and there is nothing to prove, so suppose s′<ss^{\prime}<s. Optimality of ss at tt gives h⁡(s,t)≤h⁡(s′,t)h(s,t)\leq h(s^{\prime},t). By Step 3 applied to the pair s′<ss^{\prime}<s,

h⁡(s,t′)−h⁡(s′,t′)≤h⁡(s,t)−h⁡(s′,t)≤ 0,h(s,t^{\prime})-h(s^{\prime},t^{\prime})\;\leq\;h(s,t)-h(s^{\prime},t)\;\leq\;0,

so s=max⁡(s,s′)s=\max(s,s^{\prime}) is also optimal at t′t^{\prime}, i.e. s∈S⋆​(k′)s\in S^{\star}(k^{\prime}). Symmetrically, optimality of s′s^{\prime} at t′t^{\prime} gives h⁡(s′,t′)≤h⁡(s,t′)h(s^{\prime},t^{\prime})\leq h(s,t^{\prime}), and Step 3 gives

h⁡(s′,t)−h⁡(s,t)=−(h⁡(s,t)−h⁡(s′,t))≤−(h⁡(s,t′)−h⁡(s′,t′))=h⁡(s′,t′)−h⁡(s,t′)≤ 0,h(s^{\prime},t)-h(s,t)\;=\;-\bigl(h(s,t)-h(s^{\prime},t)\bigr)\;\leq\;-\bigl(h(s,t^{\prime})-h(s^{\prime},t^{\prime})\bigr)\;=\;h(s^{\prime},t^{\prime})-h(s,t^{\prime})\;\leq\;0,

so s′=min⁡(s,s′)s^{\prime}=\min(s,s^{\prime}) is optimal at tt, i.e. s′∈S⋆​(k)s^{\prime}\in S^{\star}(k). This is (i). For the extreme points: if s¯=max⁡S⋆​(k)\bar{s}=\max S^{\star}(k) exists, taking s=s¯s=\bar{s} and any s′∈S⋆​(k′)s^{\prime}\in S^{\star}(k^{\prime}) shows max⁡(s¯,s′)∈S⋆​(k′)\max(\bar{s},s^{\prime})\in S^{\star}(k^{\prime}), so every upper bound of S⋆​(k′)S^{\star}(k^{\prime}) is at least s¯\bar{s}; likewise min⁡S⋆​(k)≤min⁡S⋆​(k′)\min S^{\star}(k)\leq\min S^{\star}(k^{\prime}) whenever both minima exist.

Step 5 (The optimal ratio). For each fixed ss, h⁡(s,k)=a⁡(s)+b⁡(s)/kh(s,k)=a(s)+b(s)/k is non-increasing in kk because b⁡(s)≥0b(s)\geq 0. A pointwise minimum of non-increasing functions is non-increasing, so h⋆​(k)=mins⁡h⁡(s,k)h^{\star}(k)=\min_{s}h(s,k) is non-increasing in kk, and the maximal ratio K/(1+h⋆​(k))K/(1+h^{\star}(k)) is non-decreasing in kk. This is (ii). ∎

Remark. The monotonicity assumption on cpred/(1−fn)c_{\text{pred}}/(1-\mathrm{fn}) is mild: 1−fn1-\mathrm{fn} lies in (0,1](0,1] and can rise at most to one, while the scoring cost grows roughly in proportion to System 1’s size. If it fails, the conclusion can fail too, since a larger predictor both more accurate and relatively cheaper per recalled utility-relevant candidate could become optimal only at small kk. The assumption that error rates do not depend on kk is the substantive one, discussed after the proposition.

A.11  Proof of Proposition 24

Proposition 24 (restated). Suppose (a) unconditional training follows a loss curve ℒbase​(𝒞)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathcal{C}) on a pool whose density of utility-relevant interactions is a constant ρu∈(0,1]\rho_{u}\in(0,1]; (b) dead interactions leave the learner unchanged; (c) progress depends only on the utility-relevant interactions executed, whose distribution and order the selection policy preserves; and (d) the selection policy is perfect, prediction is free, and executions cost the same. Then

ℒCI​(𝒞)=ℒbase​(𝒞/ρu),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CI}}(\mathcal{C})\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}\!\left(\mathcal{C}/\rho_{u}\right), (56)

i.e. on a log-compute axis the conditional curve is the unconditional one shifted left by ln⁡(1/ρu)\ln(1/\rho_{u}).

Proof.

Step 1 (Unconditional informative compute). By (a) and (d), each unit of compute executes candidates of equal cost, a fraction ρu\rho_{u} of which are utility-relevant. Unconditional training at compute 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} therefore spends informative compute ρu​𝒞′\rho_{u}\mathcal{C}^{\prime} (the integral of Eq. (54) with ρuexec≡ρu\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{exec}}\equiv\rho_{u}).

Step 2 (Conditional informative compute). By (d), the gate executes only utility-relevant candidates at no screening cost, so conditional training at compute 𝒞\mathcal{C} spends informative compute 𝒞\mathcal{C} (ρuexec≡1\rho_{u}^{\mathrm{exec}}\equiv 1).

Step 3 (Only informative compute matters). By (b), executing a dead candidate leaves the learner unchanged, and by (c) the learner’s state depends only on the utility-relevant interactions executed, whose distribution and order are the same in both regimes. Two runs that have executed the same informative compute are therefore in the same state and have the same loss.

Step 4 (Match the runs). By Steps 1–3, ℒCI​(𝒞)=ℒbase​(𝒞′)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CI}}(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime}) whenever ρu​𝒞′=𝒞\rho_{u}\mathcal{C}^{\prime}=\mathcal{C}, i.e. 𝒞′=𝒞/ρu\mathcal{C}^{\prime}=\mathcal{C}/\rho_{u}, which is Eq. (56).

Step 5 (Log-axis interpretation). On a logarithmic compute axis, ln⁡(𝒞/ρu)=ln⁡𝒞+ln⁡(1/ρu)\ln(\mathcal{C}/\rho_{u})=\ln\mathcal{C}+\ln(1/\rho_{u}), so the conditional curve is the unconditional one shifted left by ln⁡(1/ρu)\ln(1/\rho_{u}). No property of ℒbase\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}} beyond being a function of compute was used, so the identity holds for any curve shape. ∎

Appendix B Acquisition Functions for the Digital and Physical Instantiations

This appendix collects the acquisition functions behind the methods discussed in Section 5.1, and shows that they share one cost-normalized form: the scalar on which System-1 gates System-2.

Digital: scoring a prompt before generation.

Given the prompt and the model’s recent history, System-1 estimates how the outcomes of a prompt τ\tau would be distributed and scores it by how much of that distribution falls in the informative, mixed-outcome band,

𝒜digital(τ)=𝔼z∼πt(⋅∣τ)[w(z)],\mathcal{A}_{\text{digital}}(\tau)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid\tau)}\!\bigl[w(z)\bigr], (62)

with zz summarizing how the prompt would resolve under the current policy and ww large on the mixed-outcome band. The predictive prompt selectors of Section 5.1 are of this form.

Physical: adaptation risk and its tail.

The quantity worth predicting for a task configuration is how badly the agent would still do on it after adapting to it, the adaptation risk

ℛadapt​(τ,θ)=𝔼ξ∼p⁡(ξ∣τ)​[ℓ⁡(θ−ηin​∇θℒ​(θ,τ,ξ),τtarget)],\mathcal{R}_{\text{adapt}}(\tau;\theta)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim p(\xi\mid\tau)}\!\left[\ell\!\bigl(\theta-\eta_{\text{in}}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta,\tau,\xi),\,\tau_{\text{target}}\bigr)\right], (63)

and concentrating training on its adverse tail is minimizing a conditional value-at-risk (Rockafellar et al., 2000) at level ν∈[0,1)\nu\in[0,1),

minθ⁡CVaRν​[ℓ⁡(θadapted,τ)]=minθ⁡11−ν​∫ν1Fℓ−1​(v)​𝑑v,\min_{\theta}\;\CVaR_{\nu}\!\bigl[\ell(\theta_{\text{adapted}},\tau)\bigr]\;=\;\min_{\theta}\;\frac{1}{1-\nu}\int_{\nu}^{1}F_{\ell}^{-1}(v)\,dv, (64)

which reduces to the average case at ν=0\nu=0. MPTS and PDTS (Wang et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2025) estimate this risk from a task embedding and the optimization history. MPTS scores each candidate optimistically by ℛ^adapt​(τ,θt)+γ​σϕ​(τ)\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{adapt}}(\tau;\theta_{t})+\gamma\,\sigma_{\phi}(\tau). PDTS replaces this upper-confidence score with one posterior sample ℛ~adapt​(τ,θt)\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{adapt}}(\tau;\theta_{t}) per candidate and selects the whole batch at once, trading summed risk against the diversity of the subset:

ℬt⋆=arg​maxℬ⊆𝒯^t,|ℬ|=B∑τ∈ℬℛ~adapt(τ;θt)+μDiv(ℬ),\mathcal{B}_{t}^{\star}\;=\;\argmax_{\mathcal{B}\subseteq\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{t},\;|\mathcal{B}|=B}\;\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{B}}\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{adapt}}(\tau;\theta_{t})\;+\;\mu\,\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{B}), (65)

where 𝒯^t\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{t} is the candidate pool and Div⁡(ℬ)\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{B}) grows with the pairwise distances d⁡(τ,τ′)d(\tau,\tau^{\prime}) between selected tasks. The problem is NP-hard and is solved approximately; when Div\mathrm{Div} is a sum of pairwise distances it is supermodular, so the (1−1/e)(1-1/e) greedy guarantee of Section 4.4 does not apply, and a coverage or log-determinant diversity term would restore it; it is the physical instance of the budgeted subset selection of Eq. (47).

Remark 26 (Common acquisition form).

The per-prompt score of Eq. (62) and the per-task risk summed in Eq. (65) are both local approximations of the cost-normalized expected utility

𝒜∗(i∣ℋ0:t)=1𝒞⁡(i)𝔼qϕ[u(i;θt)],\mathcal{A}^{*}(i\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\;=\;\frac{1}{\mathcal{C}(i)}\,\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}}\!\bigl[\,u(i;\theta_{t})\,\bigr], (66)

with the mixed-outcome proxy, locally a Fisher-weighted gradient norm (Steps 3–4 below), in the digital case and predicted tail adaptation risk in the physical case; the diversity term captures diminishing returns from similar interactions. They share the form, not the scalar (Remark 5).

B.1  Derivation for Remark 26

This is a heuristic derivation under local (Laplace) approximations, not a theorem. Only Steps 2 and 7 are exact, and only within the Gaussian models they state. The rest is a local analogy: a gradient step is not a Bayesian posterior update, a large gradient can reflect noise or a harmful direction rather than useful learning, and the connection to the acquisition functions of the cited methods is a motivation, not a derivation of them.

Step 1 (Local model). Assume the pre-interaction belief is approximately Gaussian, 𝒩⁡(θt,ℱt−1)\mathcal{N}(\theta_{t},\mathcal{F}_{t}^{-1}), with precision ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} (the accumulated Fisher information), and that an interaction moves the mean by a small step Δ​θ​(i)=η​g​(i)\Delta\theta(i)=\eta\,g(i), where g⁡(i)g(i) is the score of the observed learning signal.

Step 2 (Quadratic information gain). For two Gaussians with the same covariance ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t}^{-1} and means differing by Δ​θ\Delta\theta, the KL divergence is exactly 12​Δ​θ⊤​ℱt​Δ​θ\frac{1}{2}\Delta\theta^{\top}\mathcal{F}_{t}\Delta\theta. A single observation contracts the covariance only slightly, so to leading order

DKL[p(θ∣ℋ0:t,i,o)∥p(θ∣ℋ0:t)]≈12Δθ(i)⊤ℱtΔθ(i).D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[p(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t},i,o)\,\Big\|\,p(\theta\mid\mathcal{H}_{0:t})\right]\;\approx\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Delta\theta(i)^{\top}\mathcal{F}_{t}\,\Delta\theta(i). (67)

Step 3 (Expected utility). Substituting Δ​θ​(i)=η​g​(i)\Delta\theta(i)=\eta\,g(i) and taking expectations under qϕq_{\phi} gives 𝔼qϕ​[u⁡(i,θt)]≈η22​𝔼qϕ​[g​(i)⊤​ℱt​g​(i)]=η22​𝔼qϕ​‖g⁡(i)‖ℱt2\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}}[u(i;\theta_{t})]\approx\frac{\eta^{2}}{2}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}}\bigl[g(i)^{\top}\mathcal{F}_{t}\,g(i)\bigr]=\frac{\eta^{2}}{2}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}}\left\|g(i)\right\|_{\mathcal{F}_{t}}^{2}.

Step 4 (Digital case). If the score depends on the prompt only through the latent informativeness zz, then conditioning on zz and dividing by cost gives 𝒜∗=𝔼z∼πt(⋅∣τ)[w(z)]\mathcal{A}^{*}=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid\tau)}[w(z)] with w⁡(z)∝𝔼⁡[‖g‖ℱt2∣z]/𝒞w(z)\propto\mathbb{E}[\left\|g\right\|^{2}_{\mathcal{F}_{t}}\mid z]/\mathcal{C}. This is Eq. (62); ww is large exactly where outcomes are mixed, and the three-state weight [z=partial]\mathbf{1}\!\left[z=\text{partial}\right] is its binarization.

Step 5 (Physical case). Linearizing the post-adaptation loss of Eq. (63) around θt\theta_{t}, its expectation is to leading order the predicted risk ℛ^adapt​(τ,θt)\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{adapt}}(\tau;\theta_{t}), and the spread of this linear predictor under qϕq_{\phi} is σϕ​(τ)\sigma_{\phi}(\tau). An optimistic (upper-confidence) estimate of the risk is then ℛ^adapt+γ​σϕ\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{adapt}}+\gamma\sigma_{\phi}, the per-task score of MPTS, and a posterior sample ℛ~adapt\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{adapt}}, as summed in Eq. (65), is its randomized counterpart; with roughly constant simulator cost, dividing by 𝒞\mathcal{C} does not change the ranking.

Step 6 (Where the diversity term does not come from). For a batch, the summed update ∑iΔ​θ​(i)\sum_{i}\Delta\theta(i) in Eq. (67) produces cross terms η2​g​(i)⊤​ℱt​g​(j)\eta^{2}g(i)^{\top}\mathcal{F}_{t}\,g(j), which are positive when updates align. The mean-shift approximation therefore does not produce a redundancy penalty.

Step 7 (Where it does come from). Redundancy comes from covariance contraction, which Step 2 neglected. In the linear-Gaussian model oi=g​(i)⊤​θ+εio_{i}=g(i)^{\top}\theta+\varepsilon_{i} with εi∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) conditionally independent given θ\theta, the information gained by adding ii after a set SS is

I⁡(θ;oi∣oS)=12​ln⁡(1+σ−2​g​(i)⊤​ΣS​g​(i)),I(\theta;o_{i}\mid o_{S})=\tfrac{1}{2}\ln\bigl(1+\sigma^{-2}g(i)^{\top}\Sigma_{S}\,g(i)\bigr),

where ΣS\Sigma_{S} is the posterior covariance after SS. Since ΣS\Sigma_{S} shrinks along the directions g⁡(j)g(j), j∈Sj\in S, already probed, this marginal gain falls as g⁡(i)g(i) aligns with the selected interactions. Information gain is thus submodular in the executed set of this linear-Gaussian model; nothing here shows that the task utility of a generic language model or embodied agent is submodular, and the subset diversity term μ​Div​(ℬ)\mu\,\mathrm{Div}(\mathcal{B}) in Eq. (65) is a cheap proxy for this diminishing return, though a pairwise-distance sum is not itself submodular.
